div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Queen Alexandra's Maids of Honour.—The Queen's Maids of Honour have not only to be excellent musicians but thorough linguists, as part of their duty is to look after the ladies-in-waiting of any foreign royalties who may be visiting the Court. Sometimes the foreign lady- in-waiting does not speak our language at all, but in any case the Qttden's maids are expected to converse with her, in her own tongue, and when not otherwise "commanded" ride or drive with her and keep her well amused. The lady-in-waiting on the Empress Marie of Russia—a young unmarried woman—has been out and about a great deal in London, the Royal sisters preferr- ing as usual, to be as much alone as post ible. Sir W. S. Gilbert in a new Collaboration.—Lovers of the incomparable series of Savoy light operas, will be interested to know that Sir W. S. Gilbert is collaborat- ing with Mr. German, the well-known composer, on a new work. It is more than twelve years since the last of the Savoy operas appeared. The Grand Duke,— which was produced in 1896. Sir Arthur Sullivan died some four years later, and with the lapte of time, it -was scarcely expected that Sir %V. S. Gilbert would write the" book" to the music of another composer. That however is understood to be the case, and if so the work will be welcomed in all quarters. Mr. German is a native of Whitchurch, Salop, end studied at the Royal Academy of Music. The starting point of his career was composiug the incidental music to Henry VIII, for the late Sir Henry Irving. A Suffrage Play.—Miss Cicely Hamilton is the author of an amusing skit called "How the Vote was Won," which the Actresses Suffrage Leagueis to pre- sent as a Suffrage play. There are many women who do not want the added duties of citizenship thrust upon them, but Miss Hamilton anticipates, and record- ing imaginars future hittory says "altar years of argu- ment, agitation and propaganda," it dawned upon the women of tit:a country that the belief that they were kept alive by the ceaseless exertic as of their menfolk. was a delusion. They then set themselves to expose this fallacy by a simple object lesson, and working women of every grade, wage earners, and professionals, struck work, and demanded to be kept by their nearest male relative until such time as the State recognised that this part in the national life entitled thern.to the -vote. That is the state of things of which Miss Hamilton pictures the future record, and it is obviously a situation whit h binds itself to many ludicrous diffi- culties in which one cad all find themselves, when -women in a body cease to work and demand to be cared for like children.

The Crinoline on the Stage.—Some concern, almost suggestive of a crinoline scare, lies teen aroused by the presentation of a play in London in early Victorian dresses. 'I he interest is probal ly due to the fact that -the "Directoire" days are numbered together with the expectation that Dame Fashion will fly to the ether extreme of full Eki rts, frills and flowers. The last serious crinoline scare was in 1893, when Mrs. Stannard (John Strange Winter) organised a "No Crinoline Leogue," but we have been so often threatened with a return of the crinoline, the polanaise, and corkscrew curls that the talk of a revival of these relics of the past has ceased to have eny terrors for us. It is, how- ever, possible that, like the wolf in the story,they, or some of them, may come at last. To most of us the idea of a return to modes of half a century ago' is eneugh to "make our flesh creep." but there are not a few women sho think the early Victorian fashion very becoming. and would not he at all loth to see them revived.

_ The Latest Sleeve.—lt has been said Dame Fashion -plays her worst freaks off upon the arms, and when contemplating the newest sleeves, one has no longer any dcubts concerning the statement. For the new sleeves, otherwise quite tight and plain, show one puff at the elbow, the puff affording a curiously deformed appearance. This, of all the fashions in sleeves, may be said to be the worst, the perfectly plain upper portion and '• bag 'from elbow to wrist perhaps coming next in ugliness, nod gtneral undesirability. The most becoming sleeve is the moderate puff from shoulder to elbow, and from thence closely fitting. The All-Black Toilette.—The prevalence of the all- black evening gown has led ton discussion as to whether it is as universally becoming as the mere man would base us believe. Many leading modistes hold the opinion that unrelieved black can only be worn success- fully by the blonde, and that no more than one brunette in five looks well so garbed. For the latter therefore, these modistes are introducing colour, and with a somewhat lavish hand, especially about the upper .portion of the gown. Women's Feet.—According to M. Bartholome, the well-known Frinch sculptor, nothing in woman is more deformed than her feet. That Opinion is shared by many artists and sculptors who hold modern style ol footgear responsible for these deformities. The toes are crushed together, the instep twisted, and other roir.or deformities are mused I.y,- boots which are worn not for comfort hut for their eutward attractiveness. There is no doubt a good deal of truth in all this but it applies less to the pres: nt generation than to former ones., Most women recognize the folly of wearing excessively high-heeled, narrow-toed fcotwsear, at least after one or two experiences of the mischief it leads to. The sculptor's ideal foot is one that knows no boot,but as a matter of fact the so-called beautifully formed arched foot of the Arab is much more a tradition than a reality. Women have become more sensible on such matters and it is the exception, rather_ Om the rule, -nowadays to find them wearing bouts and shoes which deform the feet. -

Women Gardeners.—We hear less and less about gardening as a profession for women. Possibly enthtt• eiasts at length realise that the life is somewl at too -.strenuous for the average woman, and then again there is the expense of the preliminary education, which doubtless bars the way to many al-pirants to gardening fame. This comes out at about £250, during ti e three years spent at a training college. Of couTse,as lecturers on horticulture, or garden mistress s in schools, there are some excellent positions open to trained gardeners, but unless the rough part of the work can be carried out for her, an ordinary gardener's situation is not perhaps to be coveted by a woman. Archery and Rifle-Shooting.—The practice of archery by women dates back to the 14th century, and at the present time an attempt is being made—and with some measure of success—to reintroduce it. Undoubtedly archery lends itself marvellously well to feminine pur- poses, for it is calculated to develop lines of grace, and its movements and attitudes give those who practice it a certain ease and dignity. Rifle-shooting too, has for some time past found favour among women, a state of affairs probably due to the many scares of invasion. It Is not at all unusual now to see a woman who really has a wrist of iron, and who can handle her rifle as easily and clevevly as a man. The Larder.—According to an official report from Smithfield the "roast beef of old England " is mostly of foreign production. Of the total quantity rent out from the great distributing centre of London, only one- thud is raised in the United Kingdom, whereas thirty years ago the proportion was fie-sixths. But those who look back fondly to the "good old times should -remember that in the Middle Ages it was only in the summer time that people had fresh meat. When the grass failed, beef and mutton were salted down for the -winter. Then it was not until the latter half of last century that se first began to get fresh green vegetables all the year round. Ihe recent wintry month of March made vegetables and eggs both scarce and dear, and upon the whole the modern conditions are infinitely to be. preferred.
MADGE,

CHESIIIRE FARMERS AND DISEASED cArrLE. At a special meeting of the Cheshire Milk Producers' Association at Crewe, on Mondiy, the qpestion of tuber- culosis in cattle and the desirability of a rational scheme as discussed, and the following resolution sdopted :—"That in view of the serious loss to stock- owners and to the nation resulting from bovine tutor- culosis' this meeting is of opinion that the time has arrived when the question of a national scheme, sat,- sidised by the Government, for the insurance and subsequent elimination of all clinically diseased animals should receive the earnest consideration of the agricultural communit y and the Government."

div.head: GERMAN WOOLLEN TRADE.
div.p: GERMAN WOOLLEN TRADE.
WHAT BRITISH WORKMEN FOUND.

For a few weeks past woollen-weaving Batley and Dewsbury in the Yorkshire West Riding were famous amongst British Tariff Reformers, who were informed by a chorus of their journals of all degrees—daily democratic hall-pennies, weekly aristocratic sixpennies alike—that Batley had sent to Germany an expedition of five working men, who had journeyed and inquired, and had finally reported. Their sensational discovery was stated to be that in wages and other dssentials the lot of the Tariff-Protected German woollen-worker is decidedly happier than that of the woollen-worker in the Batley and Dewsbury district under Free Trade. This was news indeed, flatly contradicting all pre- ceding testimony. Until the Batley Report the evidence alike of carefully-compiled official Blue-Books and of business men's experience has been unaftimous that German working-class wages and conditions average decidedly worse than our own.

div.head: TUE DEPUTATION AND ITS MANAGERS.
div.p: TUE DEPUTATION AND ITS MANAGERS.

There is no reason to doubt the good faith of the five working men who composed the deputation, nor the sincerity of their desire for a fair account of what they learnt. ; but on the other hand some features in the arrangements were such as,. naturally to raise doubts of the bias and intent of the management. The Secretary, who ought to have been judicially neutral, was an ardent Tariff Reformer aud editor of a Batley newspaper with notoriously Tariff Refonn leanings. Before the deputation had had time to prepare its official report he made himself industrious in publishing through the daily press, and in his own newspaper, highly-coloured anticipatory summaries of the results. He had circularised daily newspaper editors, offering them the convenient choice between two newspaper articles, one making no mention of Tariff Reform, the other fliibracing statements sum porting Tariff Reform policy. Furthermore, a pro- minent part in the arrangements was taken by Mr. W. B. Boyd-Carpenter, past and present Tariff Reform candidate for the Dewsbury Parliamentary constituency.

In addition to this the Chairman of the Committee was the enthusiastic leader of the Tariff Reform Party in the Yorkshire Heavy Woollen District, and the other members of the Committee were two Tariff Reformers, one gentleman who describes himself as a Retaliator, and one Conservative Free Trader. The sources from which the money to provide the cost of the expedition came have never been made public, but the statement was made by the Tariff Reform Secre- tary himself in his own Tariff Reform newspaper, on January .16th, "Not a single Radical Free Trader sent

div.head: penni ! "
div.p: a penni ! "
A .TOUCH-AND-GO INQUIRY

From its departure on November 21st, 1908, to its return, the Deputation was only a fortnight away from home. Most of the lime was occupied in railway riding, much of it inFceremonial receptions and banquets; and only four-and-twenty hours were given to actual factory visitation. Consequently the deputa- tion was forced to accept masses of figures handed to it by interested persons, and after its return to obtain further information by post. Very plainly, thd time was absurdly short for a task so elaborate and difficult as that involved in obtaining and sifting the mass of evidence necessary to yield a reasonably full and true account of the economic and social conditions of half-a-dozen manufacturing towns in a foreign country. Properly such an inquiry should have occupied as many months as the days available for the deputation. We are bound to believe that the fifty pages of the " Official Report" are largely padded out by suppositions and assumptions in place of the ascertained facts which alone could be of value.

Take one short quotation, for example, with regard to the dyeing, milling, scouring, and finishing depart- ments in the Continental factories. "We regret that we cannot analyse tho wages in this section to our satisfaction. The organisation of the finishing departments in Germany differs from our system, and, owing to the lack of male workers,many females are employed. Some of our most experienced finishers receive a higher rate of payment than we have found a German in receipt of; but the women and young persons are better paid in Germany, and we have little doubt that the total amount paid in wages for the work done in German finishing places is more than is paid, here. Owing, however, to the difficulty of instituting com- parispns, we do not care to make a more definite statement."

div.head: WILD WAGES REPORT.
div.p: A WILD WAGES REPORT.

Again, a single quotation from the Report may serve as its own answer and condemnation : "In Crimmitschau the weavers earn from 16s. to 245. per week, in Forst 18s. to 285., and in Cottbus the females average from 15s. to 245. and the men from 18s. to 30s. We were invited in a Cottbus factory to look at the weavers' wage books, and the first opened shewed that the weaver had in the previous week drawn 405., and in the week before 375. 6d. It was explained by the mill owner that this was one of his best male Weavers, but there are no such-wages to be earned in ,the Batley district," Surely it is a mere abuse of language to use the word " average " in con- nection with wildly disc.ordant individual statements like these.

As Mr. Mark Oldroyd ,of Dewsbury very timly observed in a public comment on the report, "The schedules of (German) wages given in the report are hopelessly indefinite. The German firms—only three were given—varied as - much as .69 per cent. for weaving the same piece. . . . The earnings of men and women weavers at Forst were given in two figures, representing the lowest and highest, and they were 18s. and 28s. respectively. Did the deputation wish the public to believe- that ,the worst paid section of Forst weavers took home the sum' of £45 a year, and that the better-paid section took home £7O ? " Wages for high class worsted weaving are mixed up in the report and confused with wages for low-class woollens, under no apparent sense of classification or orderliness— excepting, perhaps, a determination to get out of the figures anyhow some sort of proof that the German wages are the higher. By way of contrast, let us take Mr. Mark Oldroyd's clear and unambiguous statements. In his own mills at Batley, he said, the average wage of women weavers worked out at 16s. sid. for the last four years, includ- ing the bad year of 1908. He added: "Fortunately there are other sources of information as to the earn- ings of German weavers, and a Schonweide gentleman sent the average earnings of weavers under his con- trol for half a year. The average was 13s. 3d. per week, and from his (Mr. Oldroyd's) own knowledge he could describe that as a fair average of the earnings of the German weaver. If against that 13s. 3d. they placed the Batley 16-61 d., he believed they would have a very cloSe estimate of the relative earning power of the German and Yorkshire weaver."

The Tariff Reform Press of the United Kingdom has received this burlesque wages report, 'by men who could not even speak the language of the persons whom they saw, with thibounded enthusiasm, and set it over and above all the authorities extant; but the woollen and worsted trade of the United Kingdom has received it with inextinguishable laughter.
* * * In a series of specially written articles, of which this is the Brst, we purpose answering the various argu- ments used by advocates of Tariff Reform.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL SOCIETIES. e.-
div.p: AGRICULTURAL SOCIETIES. e.-
Lancashire and Cheshire Meet.

Sir Gilbei t Uremia!), president, was in the chair on Saturday at a conference hold at the Mosley Hotel, Manchester, of the Federation of Lancashire end Cheshire Agricultural Societies. Some discussion arose as to the subject of the dates selected for their shows by different societies. Especially the meeting considered the case of New- church and Chorley. who had fixed on the s-tme date in July. Alter considering the matter the meeting adopted a resolution expressing the opinion that in this case Cborley might ire may to Nee-church, and asking the Emergency Committee to consider the desirability of strengthening their powers as to the control Of show fixture!. It was decided also, on the motion of Mr. Parkinson, to refer to the same Com- mittee the question of encouraging the establishment of classes for horses suitable for Territorial Army purposes. From the remarks of several present some shows in the past which had set up classes for army horses hod found them not cccupied at all or-sparsely. Others had had from ten to seventeen entries.
The meeting considered the question of shonyard equipment, and resolved that it be left to each society to make its own arrangements.

A number of speakers were in favour of a uniformity in the schedules of the different societies in the Federa- tion, and the Emergency Committee mas asked to con- sider the best way of promoting this uniformity. THa LATE EARL EGERTON.

_ . Before the meeting concluded a resoluticn was adopted on the motion of the President, seconded by Mr. J. H. Hall, expressing regret at the death of Earl Egerton of Tatton, and a sense of the valuable service he had rendered to agriculture, at the same time con- ve3 ing the condolence of the members with the Duchess of Buckingham and Chandos and other members of the family in their great loss.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
COMPULSORY TRAINING BILL
PASSED.

Captain Crosfield has succeeded in carrying his Bill to make compulsor3 the mili lary training of the youth of Great Britain. At the meeting of the Parliamentary Debating Society on Tuesday evening there was further exciting discussion on the measure and a notable feature was tbe large attendance of the public who followed the speeches with corsiderable into rest. Most of the speakers were in favour of the Bill and the voting resulted in its adoption by :38 votes to 16.

Mr. W. FURNESS (L., North Bristol), in supporting the Bill, said we were apt to consider ourselves impreg- nable and to adopt the policy of the ostrich. ,We were living under false conditions, and unless we recognized our weak state, we might in a few years be in the deplorable condition of a conquered country. (" No.") Englishmen would no doubt be willing to defend themselves when occasion arose but in recent wars we had shown more bungling than real art on the field. The development of technical training in Germany was not only fitting the young men for com- mercial pursuits, but also to defend their country. If our workmen were expected to make sac: ifices to fit themselves for defending our -shores, surely the menu- factuters ought not to object to making sacrifices to enable them to undergo the training.As to the navy, if we had to concentrate it on the protection of this country we should be leaving the limits of the Empire exposed to the inroads of the foreigner. Fifty-seven admirals approved of the national service scheme. Ile maintained that the Bill would serve the interests of the country socially, morally and commercially. Aldern an BENNETT (Colonial Secretary) referred to the articles of Mr. Blatcbford and Mr. 113ndman on the subject of invasion and said that when me,nbers of the Socialist party, which was alrncst infatuated in its devotion to peace, raid there was a great risk, the position must be serious. We heard a great deal la, ely about a scare. If there was a scare, it was attributable to two people alone—Mr. McKenna and Mr. Asquith. (Opposition " No, nes.) When they told us our Navy was falling behind in the race and the position was grave and serious, it as necessary for England to wa-ke up and look facts in the face. We wanted an absolutely impregnable Navy, one w hich maintainad the two-Power standard, and on which we might always confidently rely as a first line of defence. Their confidence had been shattered, for • our Navy hal fallen behind the two-Power standard. ( "No, no.") He had implicit confidence in the army until the Boer war, and tb(a it was rudely shaken—not in regard to the courage of our men but of the unscientific manage- ment of affairs. If the navy proved to be as unpre- pared as the army and there was a possibility of inva- sion, the results could not fail to be disastrous. In this country we were getting extremely hysterical and pleasure-loving, and were failing to live up to our responsibilities. We went in thousands to Watch a few highly paid people from other towns give us a game of football. What use would the men who yelled them- selves hoarse on a Saturday afternoon be in time of invasion? "We want men who are able to fight them- selves, able to play themselves, and able to shoot themselves " declared the Alderman and the House laughed heartily. " These yelling enthusiasts—l would almost 'call them Yahoos—would be absolutely useless and would be mown down like sheep before a fore4n invader." He did not Ike the idea of getting mer- ceearies to fight our battles. To him there seamed no adequate second line of defence except that of national service, and this behind an Imperial fleet would secure us against any attack. Ho believed there would eventually be a union of all the Empire on the basis of national service.

Mr. H. S. TOWNROE (1., Chatham) said the real ques- tion we had to face was national efficiency. In recruit- ing for the navy we had to reject 35,000 men to get 5,000 and that showed the disgraceful state of physical degeneration. Mr. Townroe quoted figures with regard to the Army. Something must be done to stop physical deterioration—for e were going steadily downhill— and he believed national service was the best way to do it. " You cannot" said Mr. Townroe " give drill to people with empty stemachs. You say Give them free breakfasts,' but free meals are not enough, without clothing and hou:ing. Are 3ou going to pauperise them by giving them everything withoutasking for any- thing in return? Let us feed themtimhen they are out in camp, but let them do their duty in return." National service, he maintained, would give everybody a chance. It was the greatest democratic proposal ever brought before the country and yet Liberal members last week treated the question with flippancy. He was ashamed at the attitude of the Irish Party on this question. National service was a great physical and moral reform and he begged them to put prejudice aside and face this question fairly and squarely. Mr. H. G. ROBERTS (L., Montgomery Boroughs) said the foremost reason why he supported the Bill was that unless we had a sufficiently large force available for home defence, the Navy would not be free to do the work which it ought to do in war time—guard our "commerce and menace the ports and harbours of the enemy. Unless -we had a strong socond line of defence the Navy would be tied to our shores. The training which the Territorials now received was insufficient to meet the invader. He also supported the Bill because it would result in the physique of the working people being improved.

Mi.:. WI NIGHTINGALE (S., Normanton) said there were millions of people in this country without hope. If we went to them and said " We want a Territorial Army to keep the invader out" they would say "What invader would make our position any worse?" Who was behind this movement? He said fearlessly that German and Jew financiers in this country were financing it, and not for the people's wAlbeing. (Laughter). The Boer War was not for the people's good. With regard to physical degeneration, the rejections from the German Army were 46 per cent. snd from the Swiss Army 42 per cent. If the capitalists of this country would pay a fair living wage and troat the children as a national asset, we should hive a strong, irile manhood. If we had not a good navy at present, there must have been some splendid jobbery sod robbery, for we had paid enough for it. Mr. J. H. SMETHURST (C.. Bolton) raid he WtiS glad this was a non-party Bill. He looked forward to the time when there would be no parties, when the people would be united for the common good, and national service would tend to that end. This !ins a splendid Bill and reflected the. old I4tal .mocao, "Peace, retrenchment and reform." -

INfr. JOHNSTONE (L., Duchies) said Captain Gros- field's speech did not consist of argument, level-headed- ness and cool juOgment, but a collection of illogical ideas mixed with funk and holy fear of the German bogey. (Laughter.) The Bill would compel the young men of thecountry to submit to a military autocracy, and in many cases to be treated as dogs. No man would con psi him to take arms, and no man would take away his right as an Englishman to liberty. Treat men sympathetically and feed them properly, and we should have a volunteer force equal to all necessities. Com- pulsory training would be a millstone round the reek of this country. it would choke the breath of liberty and turn the spirit of manfulne=s and self-reliance, characteristic of Englishmen, into one of subjection and deg. adat ion.

Mr. E. J. HALL (C., Gloucester, N.) supported the Bill on the ground of individual duty towards the nation. (Hear, Lear.) Why should it be the duty of any one man more than another to take upon his shoulder the burden of national defence? He supported the Bill on physical grounds, because the discipline and training in camp would be highly beneficial to the youth of the community,and he supported it perhaps more strongly than any other reason because he believed it would be the greatest guarantee of peace. There was nothing like we tkness, vacillation, and a slate of unpreparedness to tempt the foe to snatch en advantage. Captain CROSFIELD (1., Rochdale), in replying to the debate, said be admitted there was terrible Buffeting in the count r, and when he was asked what those people ' bad to fight for, he confessed it was difficult to answer. He believed, however, that a scheme of military training would greatly improve the cc nditions of the poor. It was national service in Germany which caused tbat country to pass fact ory laws, owing to the falling away in recruits due to their not fulfilling the requirements of enlistment. He elieved national service would do much in the, way. of social reform and that the rich would do far more than at present to get to understand and work for the lower classes. The meml.er for Burton-on-Trent (Mr. Jarman) had remarked that the whole scheme meant " Pay ! pay ! pay ! " If this country were conquered it would indeed be "pay ! pay ! pay !" The only thing that the Germans ever regretted about their war with France was that they only claimed an indemnity of £200,000,000. If this country were con- quered,rm indemnity of £2,000,000,000 would be claimed, and it would then be "Pay ! pay! pay ! " To ask the Territorials as they were at present—practically untraired—to fight our battles would •be simply slaughter. He appealed to all to rally round and help Lord Roberts, before it was too late, to hr;ng in this reform.

The amendment that the Bill be read six months hence Ives then put and a division being challenged by the Nationalists, it was defeated by 38 votes to 16. The Bill was then approved. Next Tuesday the House will consider a vote of censure on the Government introduced by the Nationalists.

div.head: [By Redcap.]
div.p: [By Redcap.]
THE BEST BREEDS TO KEEP.

In introducing the poultry column to my readers. I want to say that for some weeks at least I shall con- fine my remarks to Utility Poultry Farming, and as the breeding. season is now so far advanced I shall lose no time m advising those of my readers who are undecided as to what variety they should go in for.

_ MONEY WE OUGHT TO HAVE HERE. But before getting to our subject proper, just let me say a word as a note of warning to the English farmer. It is a fact that we spend several million pounds annually on foreign eggs and while I admit the home comitry labours under certain disadvantages such as climate, high rents, and high railway rates, I contend that by the adoption of a more scientific and systematic method of poultry. farming it could be made a very profitable British industry, and some of those millions sent abroad could be kept at home. The careless manner in which this part of the Engli-di farmer's business is conducted accounts for much loss. A farmer would never dream of allowing any other part of his stock to exist and breed in the slipshod fashion that he allows his poultry stock to do. .In the breeding of his cattle for given purposes he is most careful in selecting only the best. If he wants stock for a good -milk supply he selects and breeds aecord- ingly ; if on the other hand he breeds for the beef market he selects the best breeds for that purpose. And so I contend that if the same care and attention were given to farming the English farmer would soon find that this much neglected branch of industry would pay, for he has many advantages over the small poultry farmer in the shape of good housing accommodation and a ready supply of home grown food 'stuffs, and also a ready method,of carrying his produce to the nearest market town. - SELECTIONS FOR THE BACK-YARD FARMER. But, while I have given some little space in drawing the attention of the English farmer to these facts, I shall • not overlook the suburban and backyard poultry farmer, because :many of my readers are poultry farmers of that class and very often are the most successful as a result of greater care and attention, than others whose stock is so much larger in numbers, but neglected in the way I have already pointed out. I shall, therefore, give you a number of the best breeds and leave you to select according to your own judgment and the conditions under which you may be situ .ted. I shall name them in four sections, The non-sitters or light breeds ; the sitters or heavy breeds ; the best first crosses for table purposes ; and the best first crosses for all round purposes. The best non-sitters are as follows :—Anconas, Andalusians, Black Minorcas, Black, Buff, Brown and •White Leghorns, Houdans, and Redcaps. Any and all of the above breeds will do well on a free range and they also stand confinement well. They are prolific layers of large, white-shelled eggs and are especially adapted for • egg production, being rather too light in construction for table purposes. . The varieties that I shall recommend for town runs are Black Minorcas, Anconas, Andalusians, and Black Leghorns, chiefly because of their dark plumage, as they do not show the effects of dirt and smoke so prevalent in an industrial centre. If kept under healthy conditions *se breeds will be found very profitable to keep. The heavy or sitting breeds I Shall recommend are as follows: Croad LangshanS, FaVerolles, Buff, Black and White Orpingtons, Silver, Golden, Black and White Wyandottes, Black and Barred Plymouth Rocks, and Bralunas.

The best varieties of the heavy breeds for town runs are Croad Langshans, Black and Barred Plymouth Rocks, and Black Wyandottes, but I do not recom- mend heavy breeds at all unless great care is taken not to overfeed, as your fowls soon become fat and lazy, and while they may look the picture of health the amateur often wonders why his egg basket is empty. When you have overfeeding you can never expect a good egg supply, and very often the one who supplied you with the breed is blamed when it is the result of overfeeding and other preventible causes, which I hope to explain in succeeding articles. . Most of the heavy varieties lay , a brown-shelled egg, and 'while there is no virtue in the ccilour of the shell they certainly, add to the appetising aspect of the egg basket, for nothing looks much better than a mixed coloured basket of nice clean eggs. Of the varieties I have mentioned Ale broad lAngshans, Black Orpingtons, and Plymouth Rocks lay the darkest coloured eggs. If your desire is for eggs of both 'Colours and your accommodation for .keeping poultry is limited then I Should reccommend a few each of the sitters and non-sitters according to the space at your disposal.
A WORD ON CROSS-BREEDS,

And now a word on cross-breeds, which I will give in two sections :—General Purpose fowl and Table birds. Some of the pure breeds and especially the Fayerolle and Orpington are almost equal to many of the first crosses as a general purpose fowl. But I prefer first cross for the purposes I shall name. . I want first to point out that whenl write of cross-breeds I do not mean Mongrels or common Barndoor fowls. What Ido mean is this—a first cross on the mating together of two pure breeds, the.progeny of which is the first cross. And I shall take the best !first crosses for general purposes first, namely, Leghorn-Rock, Minorca-Langshan, • Houdan-Buff Orpington, Leghorn-Orpington, Leghorn-Wyandotte Ancona-Croad Langshans, Andalusian-Rock. These are the very best first cross for a full egg basket and an acceptable table bird combined. - NQW under the _second section of cross-breeds I want to show that these are "exclusively for table birds. And the order in which I. place this section is the order of merit in which they rank; the Indian Game and Dorking stands first, next Old English Game (white egged) and Buff Orpington, Indian Game and Faverblle, Old English Game and Sussex, Old English Game and Dorking. You will see that the Indian Game plays an impor- tant part in first crossing for table purposes and , rightly so because it carries a tremendous amount of ' breast meat and a minimum of. feather. One objec- tion 'however is the yellow leg, but this is only prejudice and is gradually dying down, and if your special market should be for a quick growing white- legged chicken then I should strongly recconnnend the Old English game and Buff Orpington. In this article of the best breeds lo -keep I do not wish to assert that any breed that I-have omitted to mention is considered outside the pale of good breeds to keep. ,My intention has been to mention those breeds best adapted for local .conditiOns and climate. And I shall be pleased to answer in the query column any question respecting any breed that might be asked.
GET YOUR EGGS DOWN.

I want ray readers to lose no time -in getting their eggs down as soon as possible, or they will be late for eggs next winter. Especially would I urge you on with the heavy breeds, as the light breeds come to maturity much more'quickly, and you can continue to hatch these until the end of May, and even well on into Juhe.

A pleasing feature is that so many of the best varieties are advertised in the columns of this paper, and I can find no excuse for my readers for any delay in purchasing either eggs or chickens for the coming season.
CHICKEN REARING AND FEEDING

Next week I shall give an article -on—CiiCken rearing and feeding, with the hope that I may assist my readers to have a successful chicken season.. We seem to have got over the worst of bad weather, and so much as' the sun shines so much sooner will the chicks begin to churrup.
QUERIES,

May I in conclusion of this first article ask my readers to make good use' of the 'Query column and by so doing help themselves and others in making their hobby an industrial success. Queries should be seneto the "Examiner" Office, and addressed "Redcap." Please write early in the week, or the publication of replies will. be delayed. In all cases enclose your name and address.

div.head: Warrington Overwhelm Swinton.
div.p: Warrington Overwhelm Swinton.

Warrington resumed their League programme with Swinton as visitors on :Saturday. Most of the time there wai a drizzling ruin, but a fair crowd of about 4,000 a-sembled. Both sides were well represented, the only chalice in the Warrington thirteen being Harmer for Doitell. The teams wei eas follows:

Warrington.—Mclutyre,back ; Fish,Dickinson,Taylor, and Bradshaw, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins half backs; Thomas, augers, Boardman, Bradshaw, Harmer, and Belton, forwards, S.vintom—Hillen, back liampson, J. D. Wharton, Yetmg, and flert)err,three-quirter backs; Fairhurst and Wharton, half back; Sin-lister, Barnett, Lloyd, J. Preston, Pollitt and Gartrell, forwards. Referee, Mr. Enion, Wigtrn ; touch judges, Messrs. J. • Edwards (St. Helens) and El. Farmer (Runcorn). The SA intern men started the game in lively fashion and early tested the home defence, Mclntyre saving , from a run by Hampson. Eventually Warrington settled , down to their work, and following a bout of passing initiated by Brooks Fish was•held up inches inside. Wharton rallied well, and tested Mclntyre, who cleared under difficulties, hut the Swinton defence WPS beaten a moment later, Hillen failing to take a tall kick from Harmer. Boardman sacceded in crossing, and Thomas placed a goal. A brilliant round of passing between Fish and Brooks ended , inn try to the last named. Warrington still pressed, and Shugars :acing well to the line Taylor subsequently scored in clever style and Thomas added his second goal. Half-time: V`Nrarring- ton, 12 points ; Swinton, nil. Warrington were early aggressive during the second half, and Bolton scored from a fine exhinition of cross- dribbling, Thon as adding the goal. Swinton improved, and J. D. Wharton scored after a neat series of trans- fers, whilst immediately after Simister notched a second try. Warrington after this forced matters splendidly, and Thomas but on the finithing touch to a round of good forward passing. Fish crossed after fine work by Dickinson, rind immediately after Thomas notched a try after. Brooks had raced from half-way. In the last minute Dickinson scored near the posts and Thomas landed his sixth goal of the afternoon.- Result :—War- rington, 6 goals and 8 tries (36 points) ; Swinton, 2 tries (6 points'.
RUNCORN v. LEIGH: A SERIES OF ACCIDENTS.

At Runcorn, before 1,000 spectators. Two minutes after the start Unsworth (Runcorri) retired hurt, end was absent for the remainder.of the game. Notu ith- standing this the borne team were soon on the attack. Jolley sent the ball across to Kennedy, who was only hrc.ught down when near the corner flag. Jolley, Watton, °ken, and Butterworth gave a fine display of passing, and a mo.nent later Flanagan was almost over. Bate, Bennet,, Isherwood, and Neville brought relief with a fine robud of pastin„,. the last-named being stopped well in the Runcorn half. From a scramble in mid-fleld Padbury got possess'on and scored a clever try, which he failed to convert. Resuming Jolley dropped at goal without success, but a moment later p!aced a penalty goal. Woods (Leigh) and Padbury (Runcorn) retired hurt, but the Leigh man soon resumed play, Runcorn having only eleven men on the field. Half-time score—Runcorn 1 goal and 1 try (3 points), Leigh. nil.

Alter the interval Padbury re-appenred, and play was contested in the Leigh half, where Jolley dropped a goal. An unfortunate accident to Bennett then occurred the Leigh mnn having to he taken away in theambulance with a broken leg. In the closing stages Runcorn made desperate efforts to score, but Pearson eventually returned to mid-lleldJ Result :—Rttncorn 2 goals and 1 try (7 points), Leigh nil. WIDNES BADLY BEATEN AT BATLEY.

Batley's score of 52 points against Widnes on Satnr- day is the higheet the "Gallant Youths" have made since the Northern Union was formed, arid heals their score of the previous week against Bradford by 13 points. Altogether they have registered 131 points this month, and their line had • not been crossed at Mount Pleasant for six matches prior to Saturday. Widnes struggled hard to keep the score down, but they were a beaten tetra from the start, the home side scoring in the first seventeen minutes at the rate of a point per minute. Moran and TB3lor, on the left wing, v.ere the pick of the visiting side, and they were recponsible for the goal snd two tries credited to Widnes. Wattle Davies kicked nine goals, and Hill and Narey one each. and the try resters for klatley were Sangster (2), Oath (2), Settle, Oakland, Thomas, Mossley, Hill, and Bevan,

div.head: HuNR,Er BEATEN AT HOME,
div.p: HuNR,Er BEATEN AT HOME,

Wakefield Trinity played at Hunslet on Wednesday bef,no a pcor attenrlance. Trinity had the best of the game, the heavy ruing being against good play. Of the borne forwards Sunderland and Bennett scored for Wakefield, which Metcalf improvel. Jetikinson scored for tiunsiet, Batten failing at till goal kick. Later Sunderland scored for Wakefield, which Metcalf improved. • Wakefield deserved their victory owing to their fine defence. • RE-PLAYED TIE.

HUDDERSFIELD WELL BEATEN AT WIGAN. This re-played tie between Wigan and Huddersfield took place at Wigan on Wednesday. When the game was played on Saturdayat Huddersfield, each side scored ten points. On Wednesday Wigan were superior at all points, and won by two gods and four tries (16 points) lo Huddersfield's one try (three points). The .weather unfortunately was cry wet, and this in a great measure told against the play, but Wigan adapted themselves to the state of the ground more than the visitors. Huddersfield wee the first to score, which they did through Wrigley. Then Wigan pressed hard, and after twenty minutes' play Ramsdale and Jenkins both scored tries, one of which was converted. Huddersfield became dangerous, but were driven back. After a mistake by Bartholomew Leytham scored. for Wigan. The game became somewhat more vigorous than scientificosnd Ramsdale was ordered off. Just before the close, Sidcock scored the fourth try for Wigan, w hien ta as converted. Wigan, 2 goals 4 tries (16 points); Huddersfield, onstAry 3 points. The attendance to as officially returned at 17,000 and the receipts amounted to £450. Wigan will now meet Wakefield Trinity at Btoughton on Saturday, April 10.

Turning round the Bootle men were on tine defensive during the second half, and Ritchie scored twice, whilst Dilworth also netted the ball. Result: Warrington Albion, five goals; Bootle United, nil.

div.head: IN THE POST OFFICE FOR FORTY YEARS.
div.p: IN THE POST OFFICE FOR FORTY YEARS.

Mr. Richard Barrett on Wednesday retired on a well- earned pension from the Liverpool Post Office, which he Las served faithfully for over. forty yea's. MT. Barrett began his life-work as a pupil-teacher at Wrexham, but in August 1867 he tansferred his services to the Liverpool Post Office as an assistant sorting clerk. By diligence and merit he steldily rose, and three years ago he aas appointed chief postal super- intendent, and has been at the postmastkr s right hand ever since.

THE NEW SCHOOL.

A quarter of an hour sufficed for the transaction of the business at the annual meeting of the Warrington Education Committee held at the Town Hall on Monday evening. There were present :—Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton, .Ellison, Bennett and John Evans, Councillors Fulton-Smith, Sankey, Wilkinson, Barton, Dickenson, Lord, and Singleton, Revs. Canon Stevenson, James Davies, N. Wjisjn, Messrs. H. Robe' ts, A. J. Jolley, C. E. Parker, R. T. Fairclough, H. Kingdon, E. Plinston, T. P. Bradshaw, C. H. Unsworth, G. Walker, J. Moore Murray (ditector), and R. B. Roberts (assistant director). CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIR,NIAN RE-ELECTED.

The re-election of Councillor Fulton-Smith as chair- man and Mr. H. Roberts as vice-chairman was carried out in wkat in spotting phraseology would be deseribei as "record time." In about a minute after the pro- ceedings opened, Alderman BOLTON had proposed, Alderman BENNETT seconded, and the Committee unanimously approved the re-election of these gentle- men to their respective offices. Councillor FULTON-SMITH, in acknowledging the honour conferred upon him, said the responsibility increased as years went on. The complexities which surrounded the Education Act in its administration seemed to increase and Wail much more time and attention on the members of the committee. He felt sure that the committee would support him to the best of their ability in carrsing out the behests of the Board of Education. He would, however, like to say that they should no longer consider the Board of Education as the height of perfection with regard to the treatment of educational matters. There were a great many details which might well be left to local authorities to deal with. with a much freer hand thin they had to-day. The committee must set themselves to see if they could not impress the Board of Education by con- ferences, not ()Ay amongst themselves but with the teachers as a body., with regard to the aduAnistration of the Education Act in this town.

Mr. H. liopEras thanked the committee very sin- cerely and cordially for that renewal of confidence in him. Under the able guidince of their hard-working °hair:llan and with the cordial co-operation of the committee he would do the best he could to help in the administration of the Education Act. THE NEW SCHOOL.—SITE SECURED.

At last there is a prospeeit of a new school being pro- vided for Sc. Austin's Ward. On March 17th the Sites and Buildings Committee met Lord Litford's agent and discussed with him the sites in the neigh- bourhood of Liverpool-road available for a 'public elementary school. In the end it'was resolved that the offer of Lord Lilford's agent to meet the Surveyor and arrange with him for a site on the north side of Evelyn- street at a cost of Ud. per square yard, be accepted. On 25th March the Committee considered, with the representatives of the Town Council, a plan of a pro- posed site for a public elementary school in the Liver- pool-road district, and it was resolved (a) That the Town Council be recommended to rent from Lord Lilford a site, containing two acres of land including streets on the north side of Evelyn-strset at a cost of lid. per square yard per annum; ited (b) that a plan of the sits be forwarded to the Board of Education for their approval. Aldermin BovroN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the Committee would see they had got one step further towards acquiring the land for three now schools. The Gene al Purpos(s Corndrittee had dis- cussed the matter that day and had decided that the resolution be altered so as to make the site t•so acres excluding streets, instead of including. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH seconded and the minutes were apri:oved.' TOWN COUNCIL REPRESENTATION ON COMMITTEES.
The various Committees were tlu.n elected.

When the selection of the School lifal-iii-e.ment Com- mittee was under consideration, Alderman Bolton said the members of the Town Cuuncil were pretty unanim- ous thlt there ought to he a proper proportion of councillors on every committee, as they wcre answer- able for the spending and the School Management Com- mittee was one of the spending committ ens. They considered it was -rather over-weighted with co-opted members.

Mr. PLINSTON said he apeed with a more half and half policy but it ought to apply all round. On the Sites and -Buildings Committes—a very larger and important one—there were only two co-opt E-d members. Councillor WILKINSON said he would not like the

chairman of the School Management Committee to take the matter seriously. It was brought up at the end of a toto hours meeting by a gentlemen who evidently had not the courage to attend the Education Committee, and he thought it would be cell to let it drop. It was easy to put members of the Council on committees but they were 'bad attenders at Education Committee meetings. The matter then dropped. In proposing the constitution of the Sites and Build- ing; C fflmittee, Alderm ru BouroN said th 3 Town Councillors had to d'o nearly the whole of the spenoing and if there wad not a big majority of theca they Would not carry what they wanted. Mr, BRADSITAW : I more that Mr. A. J. Jolley be put on the Site; and Buildings Committae in place of Alderman Bolton. (Laughter.) Councillor WukiNsoN : That is coming to business. (Laughter.) _
, Alderman BOLTON: I have not the slightest objec- tion. You can have him if you want him. , The amendment lvas not tt.lien fo:iously and the Committee was appoint2d as proposed by Alderman Bolton.

Alderman BouroN : lam thankful Mr. B,a ishaw is not on. (Laughter.) Mr. BRADSHAW said Alderman Bolton bad no right to dictate to the Committee. He also suggested that at the rec2nt tree-planting ceremony at the Bolton School, the alderman might have been "planted" theie. (Laughter.)

div.head: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES,
div.p: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES,
CHARITY TENT NO. 11.

The quarterly meeting of the above branch was held in the Tent Room, Friars Green schoolroom, on Tues- day. The meeting was opened by Bro. Thomas LowE, Chief Ruler, supported by the whole of the tent officers, there being a fair attendance of members present, including several district officers. After the opening ceremony the Chief Ruler said as Bros. Thomas Longsfiaw, the D.C.R. was present in the meeting it gave him great pleasure in asking him to to,ke charge of the meeting.

B. D. HlmuLETT,Districi Representative,presented a most interesting report of the proceedui,s of tin District Annual meeting held at Latchford. Bro. S. GAL( OF, Juvenile tent secretary, presented the annual return and balance sheet of John Dimond juvenile tent which showed the juvenile work to be in a sound ani prosperous condition. • . Brit:- 1 hyrtas LONOSIIIW D.C.R., on behalf of the officers and members of Charity tent, presented to Bro. William Lo..‘ e a Past Chief Ruler's framed emblem in recogrrition of his services in passing througli the v,irlous offices ol the tent.

Bra. LONGSHAW said it gave him great pleasure to be askA to maive the presentation. He knew that the emblem in no way represented the value of the services Bro. Lowe had rendered -both to the adult and juvenile tent. He had-been most faithful' in the discharge of the duties imposed upon him as an officer of the tent, and he asked Bro. William Lowe to receive it as at ken of appreciation from his fellow members of the tent. Bro. Fred Ingham, D.R., 13ro. C. S. Fellows, D.D.R.. Bro. B. Walker, Juvenile D.D.R., Bro. W. Higginsan, trustee, and W. Wright, Tent secretary, spoke of the ability and value of the services Bro. Lowe had rendered to the tent and also to the temperance cause in Warrington. Bro. WILLIAM LOWE in a short address acknowledged the kind remarks that had been made with respect to the service be had rendered to the tent during his term of office, because be was sure that during that time he had made mistakes.and said things that had not alwa3s met with the approval of the members. He knew that he was inclined to be that people called straight and candid but he had always tried to be sincere in his devotion to the success and prosperity of the tent to which he belonged. He did not believe in the custom of making any presentations except under extraordinary circumstances. He accepted the.framed emblem from the members as an expres,ion of their good will towards him and he thanked them very much tor it. A very interesting and enjoyable meeting was brought to a close ahout 10.15 p.m.

div.head: NOTES BY " MUST."
div.p: NOTES BY " MUST."

The form of the " Wirepullers " on Saturday when they had Swinton as visitors was such as to cause vain regrets that the N.U. Cup was out of reach for another season. Warrington have probably never had a better all-round side than the one now avail- able, and it is anything but commendable that rvyt a single trophy has been won during the season's engagements. It seems as if a fine team had been got together all to no purpose. Perhaps we shall reap the benefit next season.

• To revert to the Swinton match, I predicted an easy win- for Warrington, and the prediction was verified. A. score of 36 points to 6 suggests that Swinton were nowhere, but as a mafter of fact they played rather good .football. Warrington were a bigger, cleverer, and more experienced team and they made rather a mess of the Swin- ton defence in the second half—which was pro- ductive of no less than 24 points. The Blues showed considerable smartness on the attack and gave promise of developing into a good team. Men like the Whartons, Young, and Herbert in the back division should train on, but a new full back and two or three lusty young scrummagers are badly required. The Warrington forwards had quite a day out, and scattered the lighter opposition like chaff before the wind at times. Jack Preston was the biggest man on the field but he has lost all the spee& and dash in the loose which made him, a few years ago, the best forward in Lancashire.
The home side tried one or two experiments which were watched with interest by a fair crowd. Mclntyre

made his debut at full back for the first team. but owing to the one-sided nature of the game he had little to do. - Bradshaw shaped well on the wing, though none of the openings came his way, and there is every prospect that he will train on Into a reliable wing three-quarter. What he lacks more than anything is pace, and the knack of makinr, a quick start. Stimmef training on the sprint track should do him a world of good. He and Treharne have one fault in common. They seldom try to beat a man in mid-field after fielding a punt. It should always be the wing's endeavour to make headway when in possession. Return punting is next to useless. 4 lesson might be learnt from Fish in this respect.

The best work on the Wallington Aide, behind the scrammage,•Was done by Dickenson and., Taylor, the two centres. The Captain was in a class by himself, and made.openings for the men alongside in a style worthy of Gwyn Nicholls . or Rawson Robertshaw. Fish signalised his return by working hard for points, and contributing several runs in his own inimitable style. Thomas gave .a very dashing display, and deserved another try in addition to the two he got. Brooks spoiled his play by attempting to do too much single-handed. Trying to break through on every occasion was not only dangerous, but it was bad tactics.

Leigh must certainly have got a Jonah in their ranks, for their luck seems to go from bad to worse: Nearly half the senior players are on the injured list, and there was another disaster at Runcorn on Satur- day, when Bennett, the smart little centre, suffered the fate Of his club-mate P Johnson, by sustaining a broken leg. The club made a fine thing out of the Lancashire Cup ties, but since then Dame Fortune has hit Leigh hard and often. I notice that Dan Isherwood has had to assume .the responsibilities of captaincy rather a trying post in a. losing team.
The League table up to date is as follows : For Agsti Per

Warrington "A" having secured the championship of the Lancashire Combination are now en route for the Lancashire Shield. Salford "A " gave them a walk-over in the first round, and in the second round the Warrington men have irawn a bye. What are the odds on the final being contested by Warrington "A" and Wigan "A" ?

Wigan made no mistake in their re-played tie when they got Huddersfield in the mud at Central Park on Wednesday. A ictory of 16 points to 3 was the result, and it was quite in accordance with expecta- tions on this side "the border." A worse day for the match could hardly... have been devised, for rain fell pitilessly throughout. Yet there was a crowd of 17,000 people, and a gate of ..€450/ They surely must have started mining gold in the Wigan pits !
The Semi-finals now will be: Halifax and Hull at Fartown, Huddersfield ; .Wigan and Wakefield Trinity at Broughton.

It seems long odds that the final which has been fixed for Headingly, Leeds, will rest between Halifax and Wigan. The colliers are the last hope of Lanca- shire, and they have their Cup - reputation yet to make. I would as lief pin my faith to Warrington in a bout to finish.

• There are some pretty problems to be settled this month. Will Halifax succeed Hunslet and take all the honours to Yorkshire, or will Wigan bring the lot to Lancashire, or will they be divided between the two ? Or will Oldham and Hull have a voice in the last settlement ? There is no prize for a correct solution, but there will be Is. 6d. for you if you get the Order of the Cross on the " Examiner photo to-day.

Warrington have another easy engagement at Wilderspool, and may possibly put up record figures against the Barrow men. The same team as last Saturday has been chosen, viz„ Mclntyre ; Fish, Dickinson, Taylor and Bradshaw; Brooks and
Jenkins; Thomas, Shugars, Belton, A. Boardman Bradshaw and Harmer, forwards.
The " A " team have an open date.

the Navy is the subject of discussion. At the -present moment Mr. BALFOUR is a dangerous person, and he is all the more dangerous, of course, because he distorts facts and uses imaginary figures at a time when it is above everything else necessary that we should look actually existing con- ditions honestly and squarely in the face. Mr. BALFOUR'S policy may be good for his party, but it cannot possibly be good for his country. It must make an agreement with Germany more difficult than before. It must accentuate and expedite rivalry in shipbuilding programmes, and it must make it greatly more probable that in the long run the outcome of the rivalry will be war.

Various city fathers THE RATES. have been moving about during the last few days with an air of mystery and scarcely repressed satisfaction. It seems to be an assured fact that a reduction in the rates is in prospect for next Tuesday's Budget meet- ing of the Town Council. The members of the Finance Committee and officials are all sworn to secrecy, and what is more remarkable still they will not devulge the secret even when approached with the most delicate tact. When an increased call upon the long-suffering ratepayer is inevitable, the information is allowed to leak out slowly and circumspectly in order that the aforesaid ratepayer's nerves may be gradually braced for the shock. But now that there is good news in store it is jealously guarded, notwithstanding the assured facts that even joy sometimes kills, and ratepayers are notoriously sensitive beings. So far as we can ascertain from " other sources," the rates will be reduced by 4d. in the pound as a result of careful estimating of expenditure, and the fact that the whole of the profits from the Gas Depart- ment are to be added to the borough funds.

The needs of the War- THE INFIRMARY'S ringtod Infirmary are NEEDS. very pressing at present and we hope the charit- ably-disposed will lose no time in coming to the rescue. The recent extension, while conferring a great boon on the town, entails increased responsibilities, and £5,000 a year is now required for the upkeep of the institution. Roughly speaking, this means that additional annual income to the extent of £2,000 must be raised. Last year's work- ing ended with a debit balance of £1,872 9s. Bd., but an encouraging response is being made to the appeal for increased sub- scriptions to free the institution from financial embarrassment. The Infirmary has a splendid record of work to show. The following figures for the quarter just ended speak for themselves :—New in-patients, 222; new home-patients, 480; new out- patients, 1,060; accidents, 1,007; now in the Infirmary, 63. The number of visits paid to home-patients reached the splendid total of 1,061.

Warrington's two new bridges appear ko be approaching tangible form at last. The General Purposes Com- mittee—consisting, of• course, of the whole of the Council members—has decided upon a new Warrington Bridge of ferro-concrete, and recommended that tenders be obtained for the construction of such a bridge 70ft. and 80ft. wide. We were of the opinion from the outset of the present scheme that 60ft. width would be ample, but seeing that the bigger structure has carried the day we can only express the view that the error is in the right direction and merely involves an increased expendi- ture which the town can, presumably, afford. We are, however, gratified to learn that the line of the new bridge is to be in continuation of the line of Bridge-street, and not according to the skewed measurements painted on the river-walls some months ago. In connection with the final preference of ferro-concrete over steel or stone, it is interesting to note that the citizens of Waterford in Ireland have been troubled by the same problems' which have taxed the city fathers of Warrington. The question— ferro-concrete or steel for the new bridge over the river there—necessitated the calling of a town's meeting, at which a resolution in favour of the more economical scheme was cvried unanimously. The Waterford estimate for a steel structure was £114,000, and ferro-concrete is expected to save £20,000 in addition to providing local employment for 70 per cent of the necessary labour. This latter is a considera- tion which carried weight, and as it will, we presume, apply to• Warrington proportion- ately it clinches the argument for ferro- concrete.
THE BRIDGES.

With regard to the Howley foot-bridge, the Bridges Sub-Committee had decided upon a site on the east side of the Howley warehouses and accepted a tender at £390. The General Purposes_Committee has refused to confirm the recommendations, and since their decision Councillor W. B. Roberts has placed special motions upon the agenda for Tuesday's Council meeting to revert to the Sub-Committee's proposals. There 'seems to be as great a conflict of opinion as over the larger bridge. The only point we feel inclined to raise is in regard to the site pro 7 posed. Is it not too far from the Weir and the Victoria Park entrance to be really convenient? -

The Government has THE SWEATING decided to keep alive, EVIL, though in a state of suspended animation, the Bill introduced by Mr. Hill for dealing with sweated industries. As Mr. Churchill pointed out, by adjourning the debate which took place on Friday, the 26th of March, Mr. Hill's Bill was left unfettered, unprejudiced, and still in the field, capable of stepping into the breach if any misfortune should happen to the Government Bill. In some quarters there is an inclination to prefer Mr. Hill's Bill, because, in the first place, it is thought that the Government Bill would be,in essence,

only a permissive enactment, and, secondly, because the Government Bill is believed to lean too much towards centralisation in the hands of the Board of Trade. But there is some misapprehension regarding the per- missive character of Mr. Churchill's measure. After a somewhat protracted experimental stage, compulsion can be applied, under it, on certain conditions. And in regard to the objection to centralisation, there,is really no ground for disputing Mr. Churchill's claim that "if Parliament conferred upon the Board of Trade the powers asked for, the Department would be animated by a spirit of earnestness and zeal in applying legisla- tion in such a way as to secure not merely the most striking expression of pious opinion, but also the greatest measure of practical result."

Liborals are neither CROYDON. surprised nor chag- rined at Mr. RaphDel's failure to win Croydon. He was attacking a well-known Tory stronghold at an awkward time, and his chances were lessened by the political manipulation of the navy scare. Just as Peckham was won by " Beer,glorious beer," Croydon has succumbed to the parrot- like cry of "Dreadnoughts, eight Dread- noughts." Our friends the enemy are crow- ing lustily at the majority of 3,948 over the Liberal, quite overlooking the fact Mr. Raphael made a wonderfully good fight and actually increased the Liberal poll by 468, over and above the figures at the Free Trade election of 1906. This can hardly be con- strued as a condemnation of the Govern- ment, which, at least, retains the unabated confidence of Liberals and Progressives. The Tory majority was taken from the Labour poll. Mr. Frank Smith's total of only 886 votes was the most remarkable feature of the election. Last time the Labour candidate polled 4,007, and the differ- ence between the two totals is too great to be explained away. We wonder whether the result will be to induce the Labour people to adopt any different policy as to third candidatures? Here no particular harm was done, for Mr. Smith did not lose Mr. Raphael the election though he doubtless discouraged many, Liberals. But there are a good many Iseats where a Labour candidate can poll a. small number ofvotes and yet lose the Liberal the seat. If, as we are sometimes told, there is no difference between the two great parties, well and good; but if the Labour Party would like the next Government to be a Liberal and Free Trade Government they would do well to remember that an obliga- tion lies upon them in this matter of third candidatures. Labour will be very ill- advised if it continues to bury its head in the sand, and to kick out indiscriminately with its heels.
VATIVIS NOTES
"Vote for Cocks and Henshall " appeared on a District Council election poster at Bred- bury, and the local youth have succumbed to the temptation of obliterating the last four letters. . .

* * Mr. Philip Snowden, M.P. estimates that a 10 per cent. tariff on foodstuffs and manu- factured articles would increase the cost of living to every family by about 6s. per week. Let the workers ponder over this startling fact.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield,-M.P. has paired with Sir Edward Sassoon till the Easter recess. His duties as captain of the Cannes golf club have necessitated his going over there, the big golfing event of the year at the French resort being due to take place. ** _ _

Most elections are Prolific in incidents of a personal and often amusing character. The one at Croydon was no exception. One aged elector on emerging from the polling booth was asked by an inquisitive party agent on which side he had voted. The' old man smiled, and eloquently waved a Pensions pass-book in the qu&tioner's face. His vote was evidently inspired by that somewhat rare thing, political gratitude. * * *

With the end of March and no news of Halley's comet, we can hardly expect that, if it should turn up in 1910 after its absence of seventy-five years, it will be a very con- spicuous object. For some months the part of the sky through which it should be moving now has been photographed almost nightly with powerful telescopes, which would record its presence months before it could be seen visually, even with a telescope, but nothing has been discovered. From now that region will be too near the sun to be searched, and not until the autumn will another opportunity present itself to look for the comet. * * *

Every barber should have his Boswell, not to chronicle his own sayings, of course, but to save from oblivion the wisdom of his customers. The other day a discussion arose among some waiting customers con- cerning a certain departed W arrington worthy and the assertion was made that he had been Mayor of the town. The" man who knows" is seldom absent from the hairdressers' benches and on this occasion he spoke out in terms that admitted of no reply. "Nay he never was" he said with terrific emphasis" I know what I'm talking about 'and I know he never got past being Ex- Mayor."

While Mr. George Rose's lecture on "Improvements in Existing Towns" given before the Beautiful Warrington Society on Thursday evening, dealt with the subject in a general way, this enthusiastic idealist did not lose an opportunity of emphasising it§ local application. He called attention to that dreary waste land in the vicinity of the County Court and said what a great improvement would be effected if it were planted with trees and shrubs. " Hear, hear" say we, and it is certain that if such a scheme of beautification were arranged it would be much appreciated by the towns- people. Perhaps the owners will be disposed to co-operate•with the Beautiful Warring- ton Society in the matter. The land could hardly be depreciated in value by such a plan. * *

One obstacle to the development of the "City Beautiful" Was briefly touched upon by Mr. G. Rose. That is the invariable tendency for the price of land to go up when it is required for such improvements. At present the only way of avoiding the increased toll is to employ some caution and ingenuity in acquiring land. But what an anomaly it is that landlords should be able tq hold up land until municipal enter- prise enhances its value, and obtain fabulous sums for it, without contributing their just share of taxation. The difficulty of achiev- ing something like the ideal lef the City Beautiful is one more argument for that much-needed reform—the taxation of land values—and we hope we shall not have long to wait before something drastic is done in this direction.

The resolution to re-pave the top portion of Buttermarket-street with wood-blocks is, we learn from the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, to be rescinded. Why? Perhaps there will be a satisfuctory answer to the question on Tuesday evening. * * *

One or two Corporation Committees have have been putting their heads together with a view to making improvements in the lighting of the four principal streets of the borough. There is scope for their efforts, for the light comes in shreds and patches at present. * * *

We are glad to note that the local Free Church Council has drawn the attention of the Watch Committee to the sale of objec- tionable picture postcards. Examples of a particularly vulgar and disgusting kind can be found in many local shop-windows, and while they fall short of being indecent they are certainly of a kind which ought not to be exhibited in the public gaze. We hope the police will find some means of discourag- ing this class of trade, for it is bound to have harmful results on young minds.

Warrington Liberals will be interested to hear that Mr. Francis Neilson, who addressed many meetings here with great acceptance before the last general election, has been invited to address the Hyde Division Liberal Association with a view of his becoming the Liberal candidate. Mr. Neilson, who was
porn in Birkenhead, is an ardent land reformer and an able debater. He was Liberal candidate for the Newport division of Shropshire at the general election of 1906 and also at a recent by-election.

* When certain Manchester banks launched out into the " savingS " business they offered to customers the advantage of leaving any valuables for safe custody in their strong rooms. And a director of a bank which has not laid itself out for this smaller class of business tells a story—doubtless a real story —of how one customer took advantage of the privilege and, incidentally, of the bank also. This alleged customer opened an •account by depositing a shilling and immediately handed in a portmanteau to be taken care of. Two hours later he returned, retrieved his baggage drew out his shilling, and closed the account casually observing : "Cheapest left luggage office I ever used." * * *

There is prevalent among us, in every- place and in every class; a spirit of aimless- ness.—The Archbishop of York. Bluebeard was wrong to shut the door, and Fatima, who was the first Suffragette, perfectly right to open it.—Canon Barnett. We are told of "faith, hope, and charity."
I would like to alter tlat, and say, "faith, hope and work • and the greatest of these is work."—Mr. W. H. Lever, MP.

In a few years the letters from friend to friend, which Dante declared to be the best of all forms of literature, will be as extinct as the heiroglyphics on the tombs of the kings. The telephone, the typewriter, and the tele- gram are killing the letter-writer.—Mr. Clement Shorter. • 0 _ _

"The true reason fo;; the fall of our foreign trade in 1908 was not the stress of competi- tion from foreigners (says the "Economist ") but the decline in the foreigners' purchasing power. The slackness of American trade cut off as though with a knife the exports of a number of British industries, simply because the American consumer could not afford to buy; and at the other end of the world, the bad Indian. harvest greatly reduced the wealth of the natives, and spoilt the - Eastern market for the Lancashire weaver. We may, in fact, compress into a single sentence the three main causes of the depression—the crisis in America, the crisis in Japan, and the bad harvest in India. Japan could not sell its silk to America, and could not buy cotton goods from us; while in the United States both the poorer and the wealthier classes were reduced suddenly to a lower scale of comfort and expenditure, and could not buy from us the articles of luxury which form a large part of our exports to America."

div.head: SCHOOLS CLOSED.
div.p: SCHOOLS CLOSED.
An Infectious Diseases Outbreak.

On the recOmmendation of the Medical Officer of Health, all the elementary schools in the borough were closed at noon yesterday until Aprill9th. This course, has been rendered necessary by the prevalence of measles, scarlet fever, and mumps, which has resulted in a very great falling off in the attendance at the schools. Under ordinary circumstances the Easter holidays would have commenced on Wednes- day evening next and continued until April 19th, so that the action of the authorities only means an addition of three and a half days to the usual vacation.

div.head: PALACE AND lIIPPOD3OIII
div.p: PALACE AND lIIPPOD3OIII

Though there is no very remarkable turn at the Palace and Hippodrome this week there are a number of miscellaneous items which provide plenty of eat r- tainment. The Gaudsmidts, eccentric comedy acrobats, perform in company with a couple of well trained Spanish poodles, and their tura is one which appeals to .every section of the audience. Clever gymnastics are admirably mingled with fun, and the p )odles take a fair share in both. To sea two men and tAve dogs tossing somersaults in unison is not an _every day oecurrence. The Cumberlands have specialised in trick cycling and balancing feats combined, and many of their feats are almost incredibly daring Lnd successful. They would be noteworthy if done on nature's pedal extremities alone, but when performed from the cycle saddle at full speed round the stage they are really amusing. A smarter troupe has not been seen at Warrington. Novelty is tre chief characteristic of Wilson Hallett's show. He has a remarkable caph.::ity for imitation of children of tender sears, and keeps the audience in a roar of men i- meat with his child studies. Musical Selvo is one of those gentlemen who have perfected unusual means of producing usual music. His selec- tions on glasses filled with water and on the silvo- chimes were very well received. As a Scotch comedian Bob Hamilton does exceedingly well. He can sing a gpod song npd tell a story in the style of the born raconteur. Ethel Sheffer pays a return visit with new illustrated songs, and her tuneful ditties always corn. maod a resounding chorus from the "gods." Rose Pink appears as a comtfdienne and dancer in the dress of a child of six, and Henry and Blanche combine as vocalists and dancers. The biograph has a selection of up-to-date pictures which keep -people in their seats right to the end of the performance. - NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

A novel feature is announced for next week in the shape of" A Monkey Music Hall" presented by Miss Maud Rochez's clever troupe of monkeys. Other attractions will ,be :—" The Marconis' electric wonders; Siste-s Florence, international dancers ; Bernard and Weston, comedians; Bert and Dora, comedy entertainers; The Three Orleans Vaudeville artistes introducing harmony and wooden-shoe dancing; Dott Moss, the toy comedienne.

div.head: Death of Mrs. Isaac Hayward.
div.p: Death of Mrs. Isaac Hayward.

The cheery piesence of Mrs. Isaac Hayward will be missed by all who knew and associated with her. She passed away at her residence in Arpley.street on Wednesday evening, after an illness of only a few dqs. • The deceased, who was 54 years of age, was seized with an apoplectic stroke on Tuesday week. This was her third stroke, the first one being about 15 Months ago and the other in January of this year. Since ,the second one she had sufficiently recovered, to go. to Blackpool, and on returning her friends remarked how well she looked. She was the ssecond wife of Mr. Hayward, and had been married only a few years. Mrs. Hayward was warmly attached to the Wesleyan Methodist Church and worshipped at Bewsey-road Church. Considerable sympathy is felt with the widower and family in their bereavement. The funeral will take place to-day (Saturday) at the Warrington Cemetery, and the cortage Will be pre- coded by the workmen of the Whitecross Company.

Budget Night. The mnathly meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday evening at the Town Hall. In addition.to the ordinary businesses, the estimates of the several Committees, and the financial statement for the year will be submitted. The new rates will also be fixed, aril a reduction of 4d. in the £ is anticip.ted. Church Society Addresses, Yesterday the Lenten addresses arranged by the Warrington Church Society, which have proved very successful and, have attracted large congregations each week, were brought to a close. In the after- noon the Von. Archdeacon Spooner addressed the ,women's service on the subject "Woman in the Home" and in the evening the Rev. A. J. Waldron, of Brixton, spoke to men on" Science and a Future Life."

Lecture on" Joan of Arc." Nearly five centuries have gone since the" Maid of Orleans" was burned alive in the market place at Rouen, and this month she will be beatified, that is, she will be accorded the full honours of sainthood by the Church of Rome. It has therefore been appro- priately arranged that a lecture on the life of Joan of Arc shall be delivered at the Palace and Hippo4ome to-morrow (Sunday) evening by Mr. William Madden, Barrister at Law. The proceeds will be devoted to the Warrington District Nursing Association and there should be a large attendance.

Penny Popular Concerts. On Saturday evening "The Sonnets," of Liverpool, paid a welcome return visit to Bold-street Schoolroom, and their reputation was sufficient to attract a crowded audience. The whole of the programme was provided by them, and songs, both humorous and sentimental, duets and choruses, were given in a highly creditable manner. Encores were numerous, and almost every member of the company had to respond to them. Wee Jennie, the child vocalist, was a special favourite, her sweet singing affording great pleasure to everyone. The other members of the company who were also very successful were, the Misses Sadie Chalmers and Lily Nevin, and Messrs. Lowden, Gillespie, Conway and Oswald Hollis.
