The CTosffeld challenge shield won by the Stretford Glee and Madrigal Society at the recent Warrington Musical Festival, was formally presented to the choir at a social held at Stretford on _ Wednesday evening. Mr. N. Cook (vice-chairman of the Festival Com- mittee) made the presentation, and the other members of the Committee present were Mr. R. W. Cook (hon. secretary) and Mr. T. Brough (assistant. lion, secre- tary). There was a large attendance, presided over by Mr. W. D. Snape, and the gathering was a great success.—Mr. Cool:, in handing the trophy to Mr. Thomas Corlett, conductor of the Stretford choir, referred •to the objects of the Warrington Musical Festival, and congratu- lated the winners upon their victory—Mr. Corlett said the Stretford choir had put the Warrington festival on their programme as an annual event and they would look forward with pleasure to their visit next year. He regarded the Warrington festival as one of the leading meetings of the North and the committee were always fortunate in their choice of adjudicators. The choir gave very creditable interpretations of the part songs " 0 Happy Eyes" " Song of the Pedlar " " Lullaby of Life "and "0 my love is like a red .rose," Dancing was indulged in and refreshments were served. Warrington Law Clerks Society. _ _ -

The members of this Society sat down to a capital hot-pot supper and smoker at the Wiiimarleigh Cafe on Wednesday last. The Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), who is the president of the Society, was unable to be present owing to indisposition and the chair was occupied by Mr. Harold S. lionsliton. After the company had partaken of an enjoyable supper the Chairman reviewed the work of the Society for the past session. The meetings held weekly had been most interesting and instructive from an educational standpoint as well as from a social point of view, Several solicitors and members had assisted the Society by delivering interesting papers and lectures on legal points, and several meet- ings had also been held for discussion between the members of intricate points of law. He remarked, that the " question. nights " had proved most instruc- tive, and urged the members to attend those meetings in the future in larger numbers than had hitherto been the case. The following toasts were received with musical honours :—" The King," " The President of the Society," "The success of the Society" and "The Chairman." A capital musical programme was pro- led by the following artistes :—Messrs. J. B. Poole, E. A. Sanders, Fred Fieldhouse and G. H. Smith. The accompanists were Messrs. Percy Smith and G.

H. AndertOn. A Tote of thanks to the artistes and Mr. Smith who had arranged the musical prooTam'me was proposed by the Chairman and seconded by Mr Antwis and concluded an enjoyable evening. Recital at Wycliffe. There was an excellent attendance on Monday even- ing in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings to bear the recital from Ralph Connor's " Black Rock " given Ifq Rev. J. Holden, M.A. Mr. Holden pos.;esses very great talent as an elocuticni4 and reciter, and the manner in which be entered with complete sympathy into the spirit and tone and demeanour of the various characters in the incidents described in the book, was certainly very striking. Many of the audience present had felt the power and charm of the writer in reading the book, but in listening t) the interpretation by Jr. Holden there was a far deeper pleasure and additional interest. Both in the pathetic and humor- ous passges the reciter conveyed a life-like rendering of the stories and there was nothing but admiration for the way it was given. At the close of the recital a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Holden on the proposition of Mr. G.Wallingtoa seconded by Mr.G.J. Brown. The Chairman, the Rev. John Yonge, said that he hoped Mr. Holden would pay another visit. He felt sure they had not only been interested and entertained, but had profited by the recital. In reply Mr. Holden said he did not prAend to be a reciter,but only a person able to tell a - story. The story .had caught hold of him already and he thought, it was one like the " Sky Pilot " containing a good deal of helpful truth, capable of making a lasting impression upon the hearts and minds of those who heard it. With regard to a future visit he wOuld if possible, come and give a misaellaneons recital. (Applause.) WOOD MANTELS, Kitelien Ranges and Tiles.

Large stock. Estimates free.—J. Sr GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. School of Art - On Monday and Tuesday some interesting work done by the students of the above school was on view. Some of it was of such excellence, that it has since been sent to be exhibited at South Kensington. In the nature class the skill of.the students with the pencil, pen and _brush shoved great credit, and the various plants drawn and painted were greatly admired. The paintings exhibited showed a remark- able power of freshness and colour. There were drawings of the old Hall at Dutton, which were- sketched from measurement, and the work reflected the zeal of the sketchers. The carving class studies were well represented and were well done A new class for embroidery has only recently been started, but the members were well up in their exhibitions. Some fine sheets of illuminating were on view. In the design class specimens in material were Ishown, and were thoroughly practieable. Care- ful anotomical drawings realistically drawn evinced the power of the pencil with the artists. Memory works of common objects also showed the keen observation the drawers and painters possessed. Painstaking work in the light and shade department was admired by all who had the opportunity of seeing it. On the whole the School of Art is in a high state of efficiency and the 100 students who attend manifest
much interest in their work. To Mr, Clarence Mawson much praise is due, for it is evident that he is doing his best to maintain the high reputation of the school.

Silver-street Girls' Club. On Wednesday evening the members of the War rington Women's Suffrage Society met the girls. Miss Pemberton gave a lucid description of why women should have the vote. The girls were greatly interested, several giving in their names to join. Miss J. Johnston and Miss F. Beswick also took part in the meeting. Local Successes at Leigh Eisteddfod. The eleventh annual Eisteddfod promoted by the Welsh community at Leigh was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Leigh, on Saturday. The piano solo competition for children between 13 and 17 was won by Violet M. Brown, of Warrington; Mr. J. Darbyshire, Hindley Green and Mr. A. Greenough, Warrington, were equal first in the tenor solo competition, and Mr. Shaw, Runcorn, was first in the bass or baritone s(10. The Late Mr. S. Davies. Mr. S.,muel Davies, baker, Wellington-street, Warrington, an en-member of the Town Council and. Board of Guardians, who died on January 18th, aged seventy years, left estate valued at £2,464. Probate of his will has been granted to his sons, Mr. William Diggle Davies, of Wellington-street, Warrington, and. *Mr. James Braithwaite Davies, of Lord Nelson-street, Warrington, bakers. PUBLIC BENEFIT UNDER THIII CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASITIRIL—Advt. The Emerald Isle. The Crosfield Operatic Society have decided to perform again the delightful Comic Opera " The Emerald Isle," which it will be re-membered wva successful in raising .£75 last year for division between the Infirmary and the District Nursing- Association. This year four performances will be given in Parr Hall on April2B, 29, 30, and May Ist. and as before, the receipts without any deduction will be handed over, half to each charity. Every penny therefore spend on a ticket goes direct to the Institution. Co-operative Exhibition. An exhibition of Co-operative productions will be held from Saturday April 17th to Saturday, April. 24th, at the Parr Hall. An address will be delivered by Mr. 11. C. Pingstone (C.W.S. Director, Manchester), on the opening day. The leading brass bands of the town have been engaged and. will play each day. On the ,concluding- evening of he exhibition Mr. F. Maddison, M.P., will deliver an tddress.

Whitecross Ward. • The annual meeting for the election of officers for the ensuing year in connection with the Whitecross Ward Liberal Committee was held last night in Thewlis street schools, Councillor James Evans pre- siding. There was a good attendance which included. Councillor Joseph Hawthorn:and Mr. ,Joseph Howes, jun. Councillor James Evans was re-elected chairman, and the vice-chairmen appointed were :—Clouncillors 'l'. Barton, Joseph Hawthorn, Messrs. H. Roberts, William Wright, and Willism Clatworthy ; Messrs. R. W. Cook and Walter Unsworth were elected hon. secretaties. At the conclusien of the business, the chairman gave a short address and urged them to maintain the high traditions of the Liberal Party. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. Miss Felicia Sutton's Success. At the Midland Theatre, Manchester, on Thursday, Friday and Saturday last week, Miss Felicia Sutton, of Warrington, took the part of' Jacintha" in Auber's Opera" Le Domino Noir" With conspicuous success. Miss Sutton's part of "Jacintha" the housekeeper is not a big one by any means and belongs only to the second of the three acts, yet, such was the animation and verve with which she sang and acted that, at the performance on Saturday which we were privileged. to attend, she so far roused the audience's enthusiasm and gained so well-detserved an encore, that one was disposed to wonder whether she was not making " the part seem greater than the whole." GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. • Warrington Artistes at Runcorn Warrington artistes were Weil to the fore at a successful concert given in connection with the Camden P.S.A., Runcorn, on Saturday evening. The programme was provided by Mr.E. R. Roberts,assisted by his musical friends from Blackpool, St. Helens, Warrington, &e. The concert was opened by a chorus entitled" Martyrs of the arena," rendered by the Warrington Male Voice Glee Party (under the conductorship of Mr. Adamson) who, also later in the evening rendered " 0 peaceful night," "Evening.' "Beleaguered," " Franklyn s Dogge "and "Crossing the plains" in highly expressive style. Mr. W. A Clay (of Warrington) gave spirited interpretations of "- A warrior bold ". an''d "King of the deep." Miss Sara Silcock (of Warrington) sang sweetly and with much feeling "She wandered down the mountain side" and "0 Divine Redeemer" and for both received well deserved encores. She also ' sang in a duet The springtime "with Mr. Duttoti (Warrington), and this was rendered in such a satisfactory' manner that they were encored and gave "The spider and the fly.' Other excellent items were given by Mr. E. R. Roberts, Mr. A. L. Linock (Blackpool) and Mr. Willie Milne, humourist (St. Helens). The accompanists were Miss Haddock (Liverpool), Mrs. Holt (Runcorn), and Messrs. F. R. Boraston (Runcorn) and J. Foster (Warrington). LAWN MOWERS should now be repaired for the season. Special Plant. Prompt attention.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Important Property Sale. On Wednesday at the Blue Bell Inn, Horsemarket- street, Mr. Leonard Bennett offered for sale by auction six lots of freehold and leasehold property. Lot 1, two froehold dwelling-houses and shops situate in Brick- street, gross rentals £4O 6s. Lot 2, six dwelling-houses Nos. 91 to 99, Orford-lans And No. 1, Sharp-street, ground rent £lO 16s. 4d., gross rentals £97 10s. Lot 3, seven dwelling-houses in Clegge-street, ground rent £7 45., gross rentals £7B 13s. Lot 4, , five dwelling- houses in Hopwood-street, ground rent £3 45., gross rentals £55 18s. Lot 5, semi-detached residence, NO. 1, Dalby Villas, Latchford Without, apportioned ground rent £5, annual rental £42; also seven dwelling-houses in Winwick-road and three dwelling- houses in Taylor's-yard at the rear thereof, ground rent £7 Os. 4d., total rentals £94 ss. Lot 1 was with- drawn at £450 and sold at the close of the sale at the declared reserve of £5OO to Mr. John Hudson. Lots 2 and 3 were sold to Mr. A.H.Clive for £1,165 and £835 respectively. Lot ,4 was purchased by Mr. Charles Paikin for £405, lot 5 being withdrawn. The dwelling- houses in Winwick-road 4nrd Taylor's-yard were sold to Mr. N. Taylor for £6OO. There was a large attend- ance at the sale and the auctioneer was to be congratu- lated on disposing of five lots out of six, and upon the results obtained. Messrs. Robert Davies and Co. were, he solicitors to the vendors. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS 1N LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Ambulance Competition at Warrington. Considerable interest centred in the annual cam- petition for the shield sffered by the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, whi.th took place in the Parade Room at the Police Station on Saturday afternoon. There was a large attendance of the public, and ten teams took part in the con- tsst, as 'compared with six last year. The teams were Golbotne, Widnes (London an-1 North-Western), Cheshire Lines (Warrington Station), Crosfields (Warrington), Sutton (London and North-Western), Collins Green Coliierv, Peasley Cross, Walker's Brewery (Warrington), McCorqu-slale's (Newton), and Ea rlestown ( London ant-IN°' th- West ern ). The judges Were Dr. Bower, Stretton ; Dr. Robinson, Latchford; and Dr. Jackson, St. Helens. Captain Waring announced the results as follows :-1, Earlestown, 309 marks; 2, Cheshire Lines, 299 ; 3, Golborne and McCorquodale's, 284 each; 4, Crosfield's, 280; 5, Beasley Cross, 279; 6, Collin's Green, 278; 7, Walker's Brewery, 274; 8, Widnes; 9, Sutton, 257. The members of the team were Messrs. George Warriner (captain), W. Kenning, G. Kynaston, W. Duncan and S. Eatan. The shield was handed to the cap!ain of the winning team by tho Mayoress (Mrs. Forshaw) who was cordially thanked on the proposi- tion of Captain Waring, seconded by Mr. T. Weston. —A vote of thanks was passed to the judges on the motion of Dr. Adams, seconded by Mr. Weston, and supported by Mr. J. Barrow, of Widnes, and it was stated that the competition was the keenest that had ever taken place in Warrington. PUBLIC BENKFIT.—UNDER TILE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

div.p: BOROUGH GYMNASIUM. Annual Children's Display.

Evidence of the extensive goad wl.ich this institution is doing was afforded on Monday evening when a con- tingent of sturdy, healthy-looking boys and girls, who have obviously derived great benefit from physical training, gave theirannuil gymnastic display, consisting of musical drill, Scc. Alderman Tinnion presided in the unavoidable absence of the Mayor, awl the Mayoress was in attendance to distribute the prizes. There was a large gathering of the public and the display ells watched with interest. The programme was a lengthy one and consisted of musical drill with the dumb-bells and bar-bells, exercises with Indian clubs and on he parallel bars, vaulting horse, and rope climbing. Two tugs of war, aroased great en;lnsiairn among the spectators afhd competitors alike. 'I he boys had to admit defeat in the competition between big boys and girls, while the other trial of strength between younger buys and girls resultel in a w:n for the boys. Exercises on the Indian clubs by the ladies' class earned a great deal of a2plauso. Various -ffra's of strength were given by the champion eight (the mcnes class) on the rings. The prizes were distributed by the Mayoress (Mrs. Forshaw) who gave a word'of praise and encouragement to each recipient. The prize winners are as follows :—Girl's class : 1, Miss N. 2emberton ; 2, Miss E. Kinsley ; 3, Miss H. Balmford. Boy's class: 1, U. Bell ; 2, L. Delaney ; 3, W. Farnival. Men's class (comprising the champion eight) were as follows, each receiving a medal: .1, C. Sinclair; 2, S. Price; 3, A. H. Fawcett; 4, S, Woods ; 5. A. Mathews; -6, H. Furnival ; 7, fl. Cisson ; 8, W Goodenough. Alderman SMETHURST, in proposing a vo'e of thanks to the Mayoress, said he was pleased •to see so many members of the Council present. and fls the interest they took in that institution. He was extremely sorry that the Mayor could not attend, and hoped he-would soon be well again. He had groat Pleasure in propos- ing a vote of thanks_t . the Mayoress for her presence that evening, and again hoped to see the Mayor in full ilealth, strength and vigour. (Applause.) 'Councillor WILSON seconded the proposition. Alderman TINNION gild that as chairman of the insti- tution he had to thank all parents who had sent their children during th 3 past year. He also advisei other parents to send their children to have their frames strengthened by physic ii exercise; Tt 1,7.19 a pleasure to realize how much benefit the institution hal doae. (Applause). Three cheers were then given for the Mayoress_ and one for the Mayor. Miss A. Clayton accompanie 1 on the piano during the musical drills, and Mr. A. Mottram (director of exercises) superintended.

div.head: MR. JOHN REDMOND AND HOME RULE.
div.p: MR. JOHN REDMOND AND HOME RULE.

Mr. John Redaloud, leader of the Irish Nationalists, speaking at an Irish demenitration in Liverpool an &Imlay, said that the year 1908 would be for ever memorable in the history of Ireland for at least four great achievements—the establishment of a national University, the housing of the working classes in Ireland, the protecting of the interests of CAtholic school and, fourthly, because the emigration for Ireland during the year wai tower than in any year for half a century. After the passing of Mr. Birrell's Land Bill the sooner a general election calla the better. The Government's altion.on 1-I:me Rule had been a deep disappointment, and he declared emphatically that unless the Liberal leaders put that que3tion in their programme at the next electioh every Irishman in Great Britain -would be advised to vote against Liberal candidates,

div.head: SEQ U
div.p: SEQ U

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair),and other magistrates,Thomas Allen, a moulder, hailing horn Falkirk, and lodging in Longshsw-street was summoned for using violence to David Guild, a moulder, and Edwin Williams, a time- keeper,both employed at Messrs. Whymans Fouadry,ani also with intimidating them. Mr. A. Browne appeared on behalf of Messrs. Whyman and Mr. Jenkins repro- sented defendant and the Moulders' Soe:iety.

_ Mr. Browne said this case was taken usder the Con- spiracy and Protection of Property Act, 1875. Mr. Jenkins, Mr. Whyman and himself had had a consultation before the Court, with the result that it would not be necessary to detain the Bench more than a few minutes. Messrs. Whyman had very relunctantly brought these proceedings to protect their workmen from molestation in the strdet. A short history of the case was this. Rainwater goods were cnly manufactured in Scotland until five years ago, when Mr. Whyman thought it possible to manu- facture them in this part of the country, and by a little trouble he succeeded in founding a manufactory of the rain water goods, and for that purpose a large numlaar of persons were brought down from Falkirk and Glasgow. These were the men who had struck, and defendant was one of them. There was a number in court. When the Scotch masters discovered what Mr. Whyman was doing and that other manufacturers were following his example in England, they combined with the object of reducing prices, and tLey reduced the wages of their workmen by 2-1 per cent. This was mentioned to the men by Mr. Whyman over eight months ago, but they had worked on with full wages until Messrs. Whyman found that they could not possibly secure orders in competition with the Scotch manufacturers without also reducing the men's wages by 21 per cent. The consevence was that 70 men gave notice to leave work, and they did so on Tuesday,March Ist, and it thus formed itself into a strike. A few days ago Messrs. Whyman found they hat to carry 'out certain orders, and they employed non-union men. The result was that the place was picketed and the stations also. Threats of violence were used, and they culminated on Friday last in a serious assault by the defend int on Guild and Williams, who had to claim police protection. Messrs. Whyman Mt that they must adopt some means of putting a stop to that sort of thing. They did not want to quarrel with the men; they were perfectly willing, and had been up t -) now, to discuss matters on friendly terms. The result of the strike was that £1.7,0 had been lost in wages to the moulders and from £3O to £5O more for labeur. In these days of had tea•-le it was lamentable to think that the men should strike through a paltry objection to - reduction of Is. 6d. or 2s. a week. Messrs. Whymaa's only object in bringing these proceediuga into court was that they were eterm'ned they should not he interfered with in the conduct of their business, and if Mr. Jenkins would give an. undertaking that the men would do nothing of the kiud again they would with- draw the-summonss.

Mr. Jenkins s,iid he made the suggestion to Mr. Browne and Mr. Whyman that possibly a standroipt could be arrive] at where they c )uld see their way to withdraw the case. He was pleased to tell them they had met him half-way, of course protecting themselves. Thst they had a perfect right to conduct their business in their own way and make such engagements with their employees as they liked for the conduct and suc- cess of their own business he fully agreed. He had had a conversition with the men sn wus pleased to tell the Bench that they saw the wisdom of se condecting any diflieulties they hid with their employers that it would not iesult in their being brought into the Court in th it way. If that could be arrived at,hoth parties would act wisely. Next week Messrs. Wnyinsn and the men might be only too pleased to bring about another contrict.aml he sincerely hoped that that might be to, and that there might be increasgj activity and prefi-, to the employers and men. Thor- were some minor points on which he (Mr. Jenkins) might disagree with Mr. Browne, but they were not worth while prcteeeding with. Toey were only qnestions as to what violence meant and what intimidition amounted to Toe men struck him as being au exceedingly sensible lot of follows. The Chairman: They are Scotchrnen. Mr. Jenkins: Yes, but I am n.)t a Scotchman. (Laughter)._ __

Continuilag Mr. Jen'dus said tha only thin; they would dl would be what they were jusLifi-d in (loin z, nail that was exercising pelc,ful persuasion. They gave ai undertakin3 that that was the only influence they would try.

Ihe Chairman said be Bench were pleased to allow the summonses to be withdrawn and they recognised fully the spirit in which the prosecu, tion and defence had acted. He thought his enliengues would agree when he said they were pleased teat a comparatively new industry like that should settle in Warrington, and they hape I tat the Sc ttchaien whe had come to Warrington would find thentielve-i in a congenial atmosphere and would assist vs far as they could in the.succesSful prosecution of the business, which they hoped te see grow larger and larger.

Tmgalar Com)easation Case at Vgarrington.

At the Warrington Conn! y C -raft o 'lChnrsday, before his Honour Judo Sniresi K.C.,Nlr.Adsheal Eliott ha-riSter (inst-ac'el b7Alessrs. Wood and L•lrd, or Manetrest3r)•applied'On botialf of Were. Nlonks, Hall and Co., Ltd., Liverpool-road, Warrington, for the review of the weekly payments whic't were being male to Edward Appleton, labourer, Plimpton-street, as compensation for injury receivel whilst followin.; his

employment at. tineir-w(irks on June 180 last. year. Mr. E. Woell, barrister (instructed by Mr. Thomas S. Steel Warringt ,n) represeneed the respondent. Mr. Elliott stated that the respondent was liberating a hewed tube ,on the date in lte3tion when his lent hand was damaged. Blood poisenieg set in aid amputa- Von of the whole of the middle finger was made on September 11th. At the time of •the accident the respoedent was employed as a lour (r, and his *wages were iSs. 41. per wee. He had been veceiving cem- pensw ion at the rate of 9s. 21. per week. People who had hid fitig-ns amputated to eiver,d sooner or liter and the employers in this case, after such a lenethened period as f otn June 1903 to January 19)9, thought the wound would be healed and that th man would be ahltil di ordi nary Labouring weak. On ,January 5h he was examined by Dr. Sankey, divisional police surgeen at Vla,nchester, who found that. the stump of the amputated eie;ee wa-s quite healed, that there was the usual flexio, of the hand and that reap indent didnt cotnplaM • pain. He came to the conc!uiion that the man was qiiite fit to do labote-er's work. Oa .Nfarch'Wth Dr. Sankey made a farther examination and wael surprised to find that respenient was nursing the iejered hand by loep'ng it wrapped up in a stockilig. On re.coving the siockitig, he found that the hand had been so nursed for a considerable time and that the three remaining -fingers appeared to he flexed into the palm of the hand. Respondent comptaifncd of pain hot it was a sigeificant fact that when he straightened out the fingers they remained in that position whereas, if the tendons had been contracted, they. would have bounced back as soon as the doctor released them. Consequmtly Dr. Sankey was strongly of opinion that there na; no reason why the fingers should be flexed. The reason they were flexed was that the hind bad been kept in the stoecing. On \larch 2 ith, respondent was examined by Dr. Reginald Smith who found practically what Dr. Sankey found and considered that the man was qii;to fit to go back to Labouring. The applicants asked the Judge to. say that respon lent's total incapacity had ceased, that he was able to d ) labouring work, and that as the wages fir such work were anything between 18s. anl 20s. per week, the employers were entitled to a reduction of the compensation. Dr. Sankey, of Manchester, gave evidence as to the condition of the respondent's h •ad. Therewas-nothine the matter with it except that it had lost the middle tinger,and respondent; was fie to follow his employment-. By Mr. Wooll The respondent had to use lone bars of iron which required grasp. He agreed that long the men was unable to use a knife and fork it would not be safe for him to return to work, but there was an iudie cation of such inability. - Dr. Smith, Warrington, gave similar ev:dence. He thought respondent was malingering. John Ridgway, employed as an iron turner, by Messrs. Mather and Platt, Saqrd Irenworks, stated that he lost the first finger of his left hand in an accident and the second joint of the second finger was stiff, lie was, however, following his employment in the course, of which he had to lift heavy pieces of iron. William Allison. employed at Payne's sew mills, Werrington, stated that seventeen soars no he met with an aecident, and loss two fineers from his right hand. He still followed Iti.4 employment at the circular saw and had to lift planks of timber. Mr. Wooll sabrnitted that aoplicants had not dis- charged the onus wbiah his Smoar laid 'Ton them in a reeent judgment of showin4 not only that the injured wor,:man was able ta resit ne employment but that there was a reasonable opportunity of his obtaining suitable work.

His hiunour said his rulim; was in a case where diminution of an aw trrl wts sought, but inn the present instaecc only termination hal beea urged. There was evideace on the one straight issue of whether the man was able ti resume work and figures of the wages he Could earn, Hs. to 201. had been given. Wooll said the application spec' fled "termination or di •iiiautioa " and th firm had not tendered an evid- ence that they orfered the man w irk or that there wts reasonable epp inanity of his obtainin; suitable i employment n Warrington. Mr. Elliott submitted that he had made out a case either for termination or dimiaution. He had shown that respondent was able, to de ordin try labourers work and he was therefore no longer entitled to the maximum amount of compensation. , His Honour: am perfectly sntisfied that you have made out a case for termni ;Lion, and I think it is argu- able wnether von have flit also battle out a also for diminution. • If I urn of op'nion that the man cannot do his old work but is able to do labourer's work, you have given me figures which would justify me in acting upon them. Edward Appleton, the respondent, described the acci- dent—which happened when he had only been at the works for three days—and stited ihtt he was in hospital for two separate priods of four d Lys and a weak. He had since been trotted as an otr.-patient. At present he was unable to bend the flingers of his left hand, and he could not lift or hold anything with them. He had
LINSEgL) CONIPOUND with warm water is an oxeellent gargle for sore throat.—Advt.
to feed himself with a spoon, and could not wash lchn- self. The applicants had not offered him any work, and he had been unable to obtain it elsewhere.

By Mr. Elliott: Dr. Sankey did not bend his fingers although he tried to, but the fingers did not move. Dr. Smith did not straighten his fingers either. Dr. James Bennett, Padgate, stated that he examined the respondent two days ago, and found that the middle finger of the left hand had been removed at the joint. There was ascaracrws the knuckle of the first finger. The three remaining flugeri were flexed into the paArn,and that was due to contraetion of the tendons. The tendons were held down by adhesions. Witness tried to open the band but was not able to do so ' • he believed it was impos- siele. He used considerable force in trying to open the fingers. Respondent could not make any attempt to grasp with his left band. In witness's opinion he was not fit to go back to work. The most likely result of his ding so would he that he would speedily injure ' the other hand. lie was permanently incapacitated from work requiring the use of the left fingers. His Honour said the case turned on the medical evidence, which was of a conflicting character. The medical evidence on the one side was absolutely inconsistent with that on the other, and be wis asked to believe the two witnesses for the applicant and to disbelieve or throw overboard altogether and in its entirety the medical evidence on behalf of the work- man. When he considered the evidence of Dr. Bennett he found it impossible for him to do what was suggested. On the contrary, he found his mind much impressed with Dr. Bennett's evidence and he declined to throw it overboard. That being so, he found first of all that the man was unable to return to his old work and that he was unable to do work of that kind anywhere else, and therefore he was unable to find for a termination of the award. With regard to the alteraat,ive of diminution, he found dis- tinctly that the respondent was not able to do labourer's work—at all events in his present condition, and further that there was no evidence of any light work which he could get and do. His award must be for the respondent with coits on Scale B. •
His Honour alloAed a qualif)ing fee for Dr. Bennett, and in answer to Mr. Elliott. declined to state whether he found that the respondent's inclpacity was total or partial.

div.head: Raney-road Wesleyan Church. Annual Sale of Work.
div.p: Raney-road Wesleyan Church. Annual Sale of Work.

The annual sale of work in connection with B eiwrey ro .d Wesleyan Church was held this week in the Lecture Hall adioinieg the church. The firet days proc ' eedines commenced on Wednesday and were presided over by Aldermna Smethu,stJ.P. The Mayor (Alderman Forshew J.P.,) declared the Sale of Work open and w ts supported by the Revs. E. B. Keeling, John Gunnell, Alderman Tinnion, Messrs. J. W. hayward, William ‘Vinstanley, John Upson, E. J Mitehell, Dr. Ferguson and James Povey. The Rev. E. B.- KitELLNG welcomed Mr. Stnethurst as their chairman, and %vith equal heartiness they welcomed the Mayor for his very great kindness in coming that afternoon. The sale of work Was one way in which they helped to pay theie way in the Work they were trying to do for Jests Christ and for the salvation of mite, and he believed that for some years the people at Bew,ey-road by the sale of work had realised about £lOO per annum, which cheered their Lalance sheet. They waned about the same this year,but if they could get £l5O or £2OO nobody would be disappointed. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) There were certain matters which needed repair in connection w.th the church. Bewsey- road had been booming a little bit lately. They went into a choir competition, and their choir took back a cup—(hear, hear)—and not only that but they sent a juvenile 'choir to the same festival, and they also came out at the top. (Hear, hear).. In connection with the Wesley Guild,,a silver cup was to be presented to them for best attendance at the monthly devotional meetings. They ca no out gloriously at the top, for he second Guild was a long way behind. Then they had a most promising lot of young po ,pie in the church from whom they hoped great things. The Sunday scheol was doing very well and the church was altogether in a very flourishing condition. (Applause). Th;'Catarteldael said Bewsey-road Church Lad for a long time done its duty. He felt some diffidence in taking the chair, because they had already got a good representative in his Worship the Mayor. Ttte Nlayor needed all the support he coeld have, in everything he liked to do, cud he as his deputy supported bira in everything. He deserved support as well as his good lady. Mrs. Forshaw. (Applause.) They wore two good old Warringtonianit, they had been bred and born in the town, they had grown from orcliniry citizens into the highest positions in the to en. Ile only wished that Mr. Forshaw's m ether were there that day—hear, hear)—tie be able to see her son as the Mayor of Warrington. He felt proud to see that they were coming a little bit nearer to each other—the Church and the Wesleyans. (Applause.) Some 30.0 r 40 years age he had great faith indeed that they - would have been oae united Church to-day. It had not cetne to pass, but still they must go on work- ing and helping, and his belief was that some day the the Wesleyau Church and the Church of England would he one united body. In conclusion, he prayed that God would bleQs them and that they would be as prosperous as they had been before. (Applause.) Tee MAYOR observed that. he was not very well, but he was determined if possible to fulfil his promise of a few days ago to open. that bazaar, lie congratulated them upon having the Deputy-Mayor as their Chair- man and upon having the Mayor of Warringion to open the bazaar. (Hear, hear). Two members of the Church of England,but at the same time they were broad enough in mind ta help any goad and useful work. He thouLiftt they had a call upon him because of his good wife. (Applause). She used to worship regularly at Bold street Chapel. In their courtship of eight years they nevlr missed an anniversary service. Her mother was a good old Wesleyan and she was a useful and unselii,h women, and he was sure that her daughter was reaping at the present thee the fruit of her mother's goodness. In canclusien, he said he had very great pleasure ,in declaring the 'sale of work open. and he vished it every possible success. (Applause). Mr. J. WEAYWARD moved that their best thanks be given to his Worship the Mayor and also to the Deputy Mayor. It was very g tied of the Mayor with his numer- ous engagements to leave his professional work to preside over that gathering. They were also graced w.th the presence of the MayOre'is of Warrington. Her mother went about doing good and they all had a great regard for her. They were also indebted to the Deputy Mayoress for her kindness in coming amongst them. (Applause.) Aldermae TismoN in secendine said the Corporation was certainly well represented. When some people said the members of the Corporation were seldom engaged in any good and uieful work he thought the Mayor and the Deputy Mayor might give the lie to that statement to-day. He was very

proud to second the vote cf thanks knowing that the); had two gentlemen who occupied, and had occupiea the highest municipal positions. They appreciated tht! work of the two eminent laymen of the Church of England, and as long as the Mayor of Warrington knew and felt that it Wa3 their duty to do that sort of thing. —not only helping in municipal affairs, but also 4:1 attending to the social and moral duties—they Nvoula always command the honour and respect of Warrington. (Applause.) The Rev. E. B. KEELING, in supporting said if thel were true to their record and their traditions es Wes: leyan Methodists they ought to be the friends of all and the enemies of none. (Chairman, hear, hear.) thought Bewsey=road people were trying to live up to that record and trying t) make it easier for people ta live a good life. (Applause.) The motion was carried unanimously and the businesa of the sale proceeded.
The amount realizei during Wednesday afterllooo was 240.
THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

Thursday's proceedings were presided over by Mrs. A. Taylor, who was supported by Mrs. F. A. Harris, wbo declared the sale open. Amongst those present were the Revs. Thomas Miller and E. B. Keeling, Messrs. F. A' Harris, R. H. Meldrien, F. Hallett, A. Taylor, J. Upsoe E. J. Mitchell and Dr. Ferguson. Mrs. TAYLOR said Bea soy-road was really her borne Church and for heart was very warm towards it. She saw the foundation stone laid, she heard the firo sermon preached in it, and was one of the first mentleo. of the choir. It was at Bewsey-road that she give her heart to God, and she would . never forget it. In con; elusion she said she hoped that those who had workea hard for the sale would he blessed and if it was not success she hoped they would he content. (Applause.) - Mrs. HA RR ES said she aleays felt in coming te fiewsey-road how very hard they must work to get theea things they always had. No doubt, they would lolok upon it as a labour of love. Sales of work gave everr body something to do and brought the congregotioa into touch with e.ch other. Concluding she said she hoped they would do as well as they did the day Lefton) nod decla-ecl the B tzaar open. (Applause.) Mr. John UPSON in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Taylor and Mrs. Harris, observed that they would like to voice the feeling of gratitude to the ladies vile had served them so well that afternoon. Ile thought the day before when the Mayor and his deputy wer° there that there must be something in the atmosplivre of that place which created eloquence in those who had to speak and his impression had been strengthened that afternoon. The admirable way in which Mrs. Taylor, had presided j and Mrs. Harris had opened the sale el work, would have commended itself to them all. While the men did wall the previous day, they wanted to de better that thy. (Hear, bear). Sales of work drew the members of the Church together. They interested large numbers of people who c inn there Sabbath by Sabbath and who,....perhaps, would not be interested in the ordinary work of the church, and they were gradualll brought into more active participation in the organist'. Lion of the spiritual work of the church. (Applause). Dr. J. FERGUSON, in seconding, remarked that their hoped that portly with their own people and partly' with their friends from Stockton Heath they -would do better even than • the previous day. (Applause). The Rev. E. B. KEELING, in supporting the motioP, said that there was one thing at BewSey-road he was B. little proud of and that was that they were not con- gregationalists. They regarded themselves as wirt, of the Circuit, and they were not merely fighting for themselves in those matter, hut they were trying to ki? their level hest in looking after the circuit in general. (Hear, hear). He found amongst the people etr _Bewsey-road a very Catholic interest in o:her placo! besides their own. In cone7usion, he said he was gLta to see the circuit was well represented that day. The motion wig carried unanimously and the 531° was proc,e3ed with. Tao total prcceels of the sale anvittated to £lO5 ES.

div.head: IN LONDON.
div.p: IN LONDON.

Fushful Victoria is showing the way to some of our less ambitious Colonial Govern- ments, and its Agent-General can now boast of better *nd more palatial housing accommodation than any of his colleagues. And with the erection of the new home of the 'Victorian Government Aldwych looks less of a desert! It is a massive building, solidly built in brick faced with Portland stone; its external decorations are'emblematical of the Products of the Colony; and altogether it is a notable addition to the new Strand. It is hoped that it will become a centre for Victorians in London, to gather information and to keep in touch with the business needs si the Colony.
SERVIA'S NEW CROWN PRINCE. PRINCE ALEXANDER.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
THE 81-CENTENARY OF TRINITY . CHURCH.

The situation of the Parish Church of Warrington, so remote from the centre of the town and so different from the position which a parish church usually occupies must have struck many as unusual. The uncommon arrangement is explained by the position of the old ferry of the river. When the Mersey was crossed at the Latch Ford the town centred near the church, and Church-street, built wide, was its market place. The erection of the Bridge meant the desertion of the ferry and the town hence forward began to gather round a new centre.

div.head: JESUS CHAPEL
div.p: JESUS CHAPEL

Within sight of the Bridge was the Friary and here from the middle of the 13th century there stood a church where service was held. It was called "Jesus Chapel" and besides the Parish Church was the only religious meeting place the town possessed until the 17th -century. In 1540, Henry VIII., under the Act of Suppression, handed the Friary over to Thomas Holcroft. It was sold by him to John Cawdwell on the condition that the service should be maintained in Jesus Chapel and when he in turn sold-to Thomas Ireland the same condition was imposed. But the period of the Civil War with its many dis- turbances brought to an end the usefulness of the Chapel. The date of the closing we have not been able to ascertain, but we were able in 1887 to examine its tiled floors and the bases of its pillars uncovered by the zeal of the late William Beamont.

div.head: TRINITY CHAPEL AND ITS BUILDER.
div.p: TRINITY CHAPEL AND ITS BUILDER.

For a full half-century the only service of the Established Church was that of St. Elphin's. It was to the zeal and generosity of Peter Legh of Lyme, a well-known Warrington landowner, that the Parish Church owed its first ecclesiastical daughter, the church of the Holy Trinity. Desiring to see a central chapel he provided the best site the town afforded and built a chapel and Sunday school. As trustees he selected, Rev. Edward Finch, Rector of Lymm, Rev. Henry Finch, Rector of Winwick, Sir George Warburton of Arley, Sir Francis Leicester of Tabley, Thomas Cotton of Combermere, Thomas Brooks of Norton, Richard Shuttle- worth of Gawthorpe, John Warren, John Cheshire, Nicholas Starkie, George Kenyon, John Ward, Thomas Lutwych, Jonathan Blackburne of Orford, and Thomas Potter and Edward Borron of Warrington. The deed by which the property was con- veyed to them is an \interesting document. It recites that the town is a market town and populous, that the Parish Church is situate a mile and a half from the bridge and from the market and the place where most of the dwellings were built; it records that Mr. Legh having many tenants was dis- posed to found and endow a chapel for the inhabitants to resort unto to hear Divine service and sermons for their ease and com- fort, and was desirous that the same should be set apart for sacred uses for ever with a saving of the, rights of the Parish Church. The deed further conveys to the trustees the building erected as a chapel and the building in the street near by erected as a school and "all those four shops erected in or near the same street, to be used as chapel and school according to the rites and usage of the Church of England." If we are to judge from the restrictions placed upon the chapel we shall conclude that the proposal was viewed with some mis- giving by the Rector, and that the old Parish Church was over-jealous concerning her first daughter. -No sermon was to be given in the chapel except by the Rector of Warrington or his curate, except the Bishop should appoint someone, and that only during the months of November to February at 5 o'clock in the afternoon. Without the Bishop's licence the Lord's Supper was not to be administered on any day but Trinity Sunday, Christmas Day and Good Friday-, and no baptism could be celebrated without the consent of the Rector.
The minister had no exclusive rights even

within his church and outside ofit he had no district at all and could do no pastoral work. The deed was executed on September 19th, 1709, and the following day the Bishop of Chester consecrated the building. It may easily be surmised that the con-

ditions of the deed would lead to controversy as to the rights of the ministers of the mother and daughter church. This came speedily, but the discussion was ended amicably by the Bishop of Chester in 1714.

div.head: SECOND TRINITY CHAPEL
div.p: THE SECOND TRINITY CHAPEL

Of the first building no drawing has been preserved. It served its purpose for nearly fifty years, and served it so well that its limited space was found to be too small for the worshippers who regularly gathered there.

A scheme was prepared by which the Chapel, School and four shops were to be removed and a square and imposing Church built upon the site. Sanction was given to this proposal by the Bishop on July 22nd, 1758, and the work was begun. Subscrip- tions to the amount of £2,600 were obtained ,and with this sum the Church was erected. The building, considering the difficulties of site, is admittedly a good one, and much discussion has taken place as to its designer. Tradition has it that the architect Gibbs, who was engaged at that time upon the building of Bank Hall, designed it. One of the Church books mentions James Meredith and this seems to be confirmed by an entry in the accounts for £7B for " drawing and his attendance." In July 1760, Bishop Keene consecrated the new building. By a new trust deed many of the old anomalies were abolished and the chapel became a sort of chapel of ease to the Parish Church.

div.head: TRINITY TOWER.
div.p: TRINITY TOWER.

The steeple of the new church seems to have had a chequered history. In 1813 it was found to-be, out of repair and was reported unsafe. Thomas Lyon, Esq., the treasurer of the Church, took it down and rebuilt it. Not long after, Dr. Law, Bishop of Chester, was on a visit and noticing that the steeple was out of harmony with the general character of the church asked whether any faculty had been obtained for building it. When Mr, Lyon informed him that there had not, his lordship, who could hardly have meant seriously what he said, replied, "Then I think I must, make you take it down 'again," to _which Mr. Lyon said

l" Well, niy Lord, I have had many a worse job than that in my lifetime," and there the conversation ended. The steeple was taken 'down and Mr. Rickman, a celebrated archi- tect, designed a new one. This was blown down in a great storm the year after its completion. The present familiar tower rose to take its place and has stood sentinel-like over the town ever since. THE TOWN BELL.
The bell which hangs in the tower, and

whose tones are perhaps the most familiar— though not the most charming—sounds which Warringtonians know, is the most interesting relic which the church possesses. It formerly hung in the old Market Hall Or Court House, which stood on the site of the present Beef Market. When this building was demolished the bell was removed to the chapel and the curfew which had been rung upon it for more than two Centuries continued to be rung each evening at eight o'clock. The inscription upon the bell is:
EX DONO JOHANN'S BOOTH COLENELLI ET RECTOR'S EMPORII DE WARRINGTON ANNO DOMINTI 1647.
C.S. J.B. G.T.
The original Chapel Bell was removed to the National School in Church-street,, and still hangs there. It is inscribed:
DEO ET ECCLESIM 30IJA BLACKBURNE S.S. T.P. HALLELUJAH. HENRICAS PENN' FECIT 1706.

The origin' of this bell is not known, but it used to tinkle its call for prayers from Trinity Tower, as it often rang on week days at about the time when a baker opposite closed his oven a wag wrote a distich upon it. Hark to the bell by whose diurnal din • The .pies are baked, and pious folk turn in. THE ALTAR PICTURE.

Over the Communion Table of the Church hangs a picture by James Cranke of War- rlngton, a fine copy of Andrew del Sarto's "Holy Family." The artist was employed by Mr. John Hesketh to carry out this work and the result is most happy. A condition attached to the gift was that the picture should not be copied. Though occupying such a central position the building remained a chapel-of-ease for more than a century. Indeed it was not until 1870 that a distinct parish was formed. Under the new arrangement, with a distinct area allocated as its parish,the Church began a new era of usefulness.
A. 'VI.

div.head: OUR MISCELLANY.
div.p: OUR MISCELLANY.

A Manchester librarian after reading our notes on Dr. Aikins great topographical work on that city calls attention to the list of towns mentioned therein and the changes wrought by time. The work was prepared 115 years ago and it is pointed out that at that period there was a Birkdale but no Southport, a Layton but no Blackpool, a Heysham but no Morecambe, a Rossall but no Fleetwood, an Aldingham but no Barrow, a Chadkirk but no Guide Bridge.

A. statement in the book which reads curiously is to the effect that large quantities of potatoes were sent from the Lancashire ports to Dublin. The potato-tide must have turned shortly afterwards ; but it is interest- ing to know that it flowed West before it turned East. From Bank Quay Wharf alone, Dr. Aikin tells us, 40,000 bushels were sent each season. Shipping potatoes to Ireland would now rank with carrying coals to Newcastle as a price of superfluity. ** * *

It occurs to us to ask whether any of our older readers remember the ceremony of Boundary Walking being carried out in Warrington. It would appear to have been practised in some form or other as late asf fifty years ago for in a local print of that date we are told that on the day following Rogation Sunday the clergy of St. Paul's Church with the Church- wardens walked the most intricate portions of th4e parish. Their path seems to have led them from Market-gate down Horsemarket- street to Crown-street. From thence they are said to have passed through the Militia Barracks yard to the north portion of the yard of Cockhedge Factory. Thence through fields to Providence-place, Lythgoe's-lane and to Conies' corner and Orford-avenue. Alder-lane and Longford Brook were fol- lowed, the brook being traced to its junction with Sankey Brook. Following Sankey Brook to Sankey Bridges the procession' travelled bick by the Liverpool-road to Market-gate. The large area thus encom- passed was the old parish of St. Paul's and the journey around it would involve con- siderable toil.
BRIDGE-STREET OF 50 YEARS AGO. • TIME'S MANY CHANGES.

In our issue of March 20th was a letter from a local correspondent asking if any of our readers could recollect the names of the shopkeepers on the West side of Bridge-street, 50 or 60 years ago. This query brought a reply from Mr. F. Monks, who is now residing at Birkdale, enclosing a list which he had compiled from memory. The list contained one or two blanks but with the courteous assistance of Mr. 11. S. Layland of Grappenhall, we have been able to get it velified and completed. MY LIFE STORY.

div.head: EX-SUPERINTEND,ENT MONAGHAN
div.p: EX-SUPERINTEND,ENT MONAGHAN

The life story of one who has been intimately associated with police work for many years must of necessity be largely concerned with crimes and criminals, but trust the experiences I have to relate may- not be without interest to the people of Warrington and district. As my name betokens, I am a native of the Emerald Isle, having been born in Co. Kildare in 1859. At the age of about sixteen I came to this country along with my parents. We settled in the quaint old town of Knutsford and my father and I worked on the farm of Squire Leicester, of Toft Hall, for a number of years. Afterwards I was a servant at the George Hotel, but at the age of twenty-one I had an inclination to become a police officer and made application for a post in the Cheshire County Constabulary. The necessary pre- liminaries were completed, but it happened that I came to visit a friend in Warrington and learned that there was a vacancy in the local force. The next morning I saw the Chief Constable, the late Mr.. Samuel Hunt, who took me before the Watch Committee and I was appointed a constable. It was singular that the very first visit I paid to Warrington should thus determine my future career. I began duty in February 1880, and although a fortnight later an intimation came to hand that I had been successful in my original application to enter the Cheshire Con- stabulary, r decided to remain in Warrington and have never regretted the step. My parents remained at Knutsford and they now lie buried in Crosstown Churchyard, between Knutsford and Mobberley.

div.head: EARLY EXPERIENCES.
div.p: EARLY EXPERIENCES.

When I joined the Warrington force it was but thirty strong, and the policeman's life was much harder than it is to-day. There were more rough and dangerous characters and officers were often subjected to brutal treatment. I have 'a vivid recol- lection of my first experiences in the force. It was a severe winter and so keen was the frost that the Mersey was frozen over, enabling skaters to pursue their pastime all the way from Warrington Bridge to Fiddler's Ferry. For three months I was on night duty. The policemen were not then allowed to adjourn to the Police Station for supper and a short rest, but meals had to be brought to them while on their beats, and on many occasions I used to get., on a wall and warm the food at a lamp. A short time after entering the force I was appointed a member of the Fire Brigade, one half of which was then composed of police officers and the -other half of civilians. I lived at the Fire Station and had to attend many serious fires, including timber yard outbreaks in Edgeworth-street and Academy- street and a fire at the old Chemical works. I often recall a fire which broke out at Ford's Farm, Latchford, in the depth of winter. The water froze in the hose pipes and in order to obtain a supply we had to hew through the ice on the Bridgewater Canal with axes. At an early stage I was put on plain clothes duty and had a great deal to do with the apprehension of poachers, thieves and violent characters. In 1884 I received the merit badge for ability and efficiency and in 1892 was promoted to the rank of Detective- Sergeant. In 1897 I became Dotective- Inspector and in the following year Detective Superintendent, acting as next in command to the Chief Constable.

div.head: LODGING-HOUSE STRUGGLE.
div.p: A LODGING-HOUSE STRUGGLE.

You ask me to mention a few of the more notable cases with which I have been con- nected. In 1886 a well-known character was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for assaulting a police constable named Hennessy and he threatened further reprisals on the officer when he was liberated from gaol. He was true to his word, for along with another rough he attacked the constable at Market Gate, one of the men grasping the victim by the legs while the other belaboured him with a poker. Eventually a lady interfered, and the assailants absconded. Receiving infor- mation that they had booked for Man- chester, I made inquiries in that city, assisted by a member of the Man- chester City Police Force. Early in the morning we were passing a common lodging- house in the Deansgate district and heard the sound of voices. I recognized one as being the voice of one of the men wanted and we at once entered the place—unwelcome guests, as you may readily imagine. On collaring our man we were set upon by- his friends and a desperate struggle ensued; portions of our clothing being torn from our backs. At last we got to the street where assistance was forthcoming and our prisoner was safety lodged in the cells at the Town Hall. Later in the day he was taken to Warrington and subsequently I arrested his accomplice at Altrincham. They were both tried at the Liverpool Assizes on a charge of attempted murder and received sentences of ten years' and five years' penal servitude respectively. TELL-TALE FOOTPRINTS.,

In September 1886, an Irish farm labourer named Patrick Roche had finished work on a farm near Northwich and was making his way back to his native land, with his accumulated earnings in his possession. He was going down Buttermarket-street at 11 o'clock on a foggy night when a woman accosted him and on his stating that he wished to go to St.Helens,proferred to direct him. She took him into Howley Fields, and her male companion, a violent character, followed them. On reaching a sufficiently secluded spot, they set upon the Irishman, savagely assaulted him and robbed him of several pounds. He wandered about the fields for some time and the following morning came to the police station and saw me. The only clue he could give was that" there was a white calf in the field," but I was able to locate the exact place of the struggle and found a

number of clog marks. After exhaustive inquiries I arrested the man and woman in a lodging-house in Naylor- street and the silent evidence of their clogs was conclusive. ' They were tried at the Assizes, the man being sentenced to 12 months' hard labour and 40 lashes with the cat, and the women to 18 months. The late Inspector Berry had been bound over to give evidence with me at the trial, but in the meantime. he was drowned at Fiddlers' Ferry.

A -militia man came to Warrington from Ashton-under-Lyne for his training in 1:.:3 and his wife stayed at a lodging-house on Town Hill. At the close of the trainikg the man gave his wife the money he had earned, and she was making her way to Bank Quay Station when she was set upon by two roughs on the land where Trinity schools now stand, robbed, and thrown into 'a shallow pool of water. I happened to be on duty in Bridge-street when I caught sight of two notorious characters cross the street and disappear along Dolmans'-lane. My suspicions wore aroused by the fact that the trousers of both were wet, although the evening was dry, and when I followed the men, they promptly made off. I caught one and conveyed him to the Police Station and later apprehended the other in a public- house just as his mother was in the act of handing him money and a change of clothing in order that he might quit the town. They were convicted at the Assizes and one got seven years' penal servitude and 50 lashes with the cat and the other five years and fifty lashes.

div.head: STRUGGLE ON A ROOF.
div.p: STRUGGLE ON A ROOF.

One of my most exciting adventures was a struggle with some shop-breakers on a roof in Bridge-street. In April, 1882, I was on duty near Warrington Bridge at one o'clock in the morning and saw three young men cross Bridge-street and enter what was then Fairhurst's yard, carrying a bulky package. Giving chase, along with other officers, includ- ing Sergeant Cox, I found a bundle of stolen articles had been deposited on the doorstep of a house. We surrounded the place and the men appeared on the roof of the building. Taking off my shoes and tunic I pursued them along the slates. We had a struggle by a chimney stack and, the property being old, the chimney gave way and crashed on to the slates. The men were cap- tured and received sentence of four months' hard labour at the Quarter Sessions. Very small—apparently trifling—things are often instrumental in bringing about arrests. Two colliers met an old pedlar near Golborne and robbed him after maltreating him most cruelly. One of the assailants escaped to Warrington and the description circulated by the cOunty police stated that he had a patch on one of his coat sleeves. A few days later I met a suspicious looking character in. Horsemarket-street. A casual glance .dis- closed a patch on his sleeve and I had no hesitation in arresting him. Five years' penal servitude was his penalty. About nineteen years ago a man was "wanted" for an outrage at Widnes. The country was scoured, but it fell to me to arrest him in Horsemarket-street. When he was committed for trial he had to be taken from Widnes by night or I verily believe the crowd would have seriously mauled him. He was sentenced to 18 years penal servitude arid the late Superintendent Keighley wrote a kind letter to the Chief Constable of War- rington acknowledging my services. About the same time I was able to trace another man wanted for a similar offence at War- rington to Galway, Ireland,and he got fifteen years. Some years ago a woman used to frequent the Warrington market on Wednes- days for the sole object of picking pockets-20 or 30 purses would be missed in an afternoon. She was of refined and respectable appearance and it afterwards transpired that she was known in other parts as the " lady pickpocket." One day I caught her in tlie act and when she was taken to the Police Station she refused to give any account of herself. She would not submit to be photographed but when I took her to Strangeways I learned from a Manchester detective that she was an expert pick-pocket and had spent a large portion of her life in prison—she was at that time a convict on licence. She was sentenced to a further twelve months for her Warrington escapade. A sad case was that in which a mother in the Dial-street neighbourhood used to send her child to pick pockets in the market. On one .occasion I saw the little one making off with a purse and on going to her home found under the fire place the clasps of a large number of purses which had been. burnt. The mother got six months' imprison- ment and the child was sent to a reformatory.

div.head: BEGGING IMPOSTERS.
div.p: BEGGING IMPOSTERS.

There is, of courk, a laughable side to a detective's experiences. One night about ten years ago I saw a man in Horsemarket- street displaying a black tin plate on which was an appeal in white letters to"help a poor man out of work and my wife and children starving through a factory fire at Oldham." One of his hands was bandaged and hanging in a sling. In a conversation he said that in escaping from the fire he caught his hand on a rusty nail and blood-poispning set in. I induced him to accompany me to the Police Station, discovered that he had about 14s. in copper in his possession, and that when the bandage was removed, there was nothing whatever the matter with his hand. His whole story proved to be a myth

- and he had been convicted of similar impositions in other places. Another beggar distributed papers stating that he was deaf and dumb but when he offered me one and I told him I. could not read he said." I am hard up." I offered to find him lodgings at the Bridewell and he then spoke very fluently.. During my connection with the Warring- ton force I am pleased to say that the police- man's lot has improved in regard to pay and general conditions and there is nothing like the same amount of violence to deal with. On many occasions I have been compli- mented by those in authority and on my- retirement in August last I was most grati- fied at the expressions of goodwill which 'came from many sections of the community.

div.head: PARALYSIS OF THE NERVES.
div.p: PARALYSIS OF THE NERVES.

WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
Annual Meeting,

Devotees of the summer sport are already looking forward to the opening of the season, and the annual meeting of the Whurington Cricket and Bowling Club for the transaction of the necessary preliminary business was held at the Lion Hotel on Monday evening. There was a fair attendance, Afr.R. T. Fairclougb, one of the oldest members of the cinb, being voted to the chair.

div.head: 'FINANCES.
div.p: THE 'FINANCES.

In the unavoidable absence of the hon. treasurer (Mr. Robert Lowe), the accounts were submitted by the hon. treasurer (Mr. R. H. 'DAINTITH)! They showed that the year opened with an adverse balance of £153 Os. 4d. A special appeal reduced the deficit to £72 Os. 10d., and after the season's work it now stands at £64 13s. led. The income included :—Subscliptions, £239 14s; gate receipts, £2B Bs. 91. ; rents receivable, £37 Is. 6d.; House Committee, £36 16s. sd. ; donation by Sir Gilbett Greenall, Bart., £5 ; and the expenses were made up of :—Rents, rates,taxeP, &c., £59 ss. 9d. ; insurances, £3 lie. ; cost of matcher, £29 18s. id. ; keeping ground, £66 les. ; professional, £6O; cricket goods, £5 103. ; tennis.. goods, £9 Is. Is.; bowling green expenditure, £8 Ps. Bd.; printing and advertising, £l5 Os. 4d. ; generel expenses, £77 Cs. ; bank interest and commisiion, £6 15s. sd. After some discussion, iu the course of which Mr. FAIRCLOUGII contended that some of the matches might be more judiciously arranged for the sentring of better gates, the accounts were adopted.

div.head: NEW PRESIDENT. •_
div.p: THE NEW PRESIDENT. •_
Mr. JAMES I{ICHARDSON proposed the election of Mr. Thomas Birtles as President, remarking that he was .na excellent man and would give every attention to the duties.

Mr. FAIRCLOUGH seconded and said Mr. Birtles had been connected with the club for what seemed a genera- tion. He was associated with the late Mr. Morris and many other well-known men of times gone by and was an excellent member.

Mr. MAIN WARING supported and the proposition was enthusiastically carried. Mr. BIRTLES, in returning thanks, said he had been a member of the bowling green for more than a quarter of a century. Ile had seen presidents come and go and be was now following in the footsteps of a very worthy gentleman—the mayor, vt ho had fulfilled the office to the satisfaction of everybody.

RETIRING PRESIDENT THANKED. Mr. WILLIAM SILCOCK proposed a vote of thanks to the retiring president (the Mayor) and that his name be added to the list of vice-presidents. He did not think thAt amongst the illustrious men who had filled the office anyone had filled it with greater dignity and better grace then Aldermen Forshaw. Mr. A. MYNEKYME seconded.
Mr. T. COOPEIt, in bupporting, said Alderman Forshaw bad been an ideal president, not only on account of his attendances but of the great personal interest he had takrn in the club.
The vote was heartily accorded. ENTRANCE FEE REMITTED.

The SECRETARY proposed that the entrance fee be remitted for the ensuing season. He said it had been remitted for two years and it would be a mistake to impose it again at the present juncture. Mr. JOHN LEE seconded and the proposition was agreed to. _

div.head: OTHER ELECTIONS.
div.p: OTHER ELECTIONS.

Mr. Robert Lowe and Mr. R. H. Daintith were re-elected hon. treasurer and assistant hon. treasurer respectively. Mr. C. H. UNSWORTH was re-elected secretary, and in responding said he had held the office for seventeen years. Although his interests so far as sport was concerned were now largely occupied with golf, the Cricket Club bad a warm place in his heart, and be took as great an interest in it as ever he did. Other appointments were made as follows :—Watch secretary, Mr. W. H. Podmore ; captain of first eleven, Mr. B. Silcock ; sub-captain, Mr. William Richardson, jun.; captain of second eleven, Mr. Sydney Baxter; secretary of bowling club, Mr. Thomas Cooper; captain of bowling club, Mr. R. T. Fairclough ; auditor, Alder- man Tinnion; secretary of tennis clnb, Mr. C. H. Hands; committee: cricket, Messrs. .1. W. Bibby, %V. Richardson, jun., B. Silcnck, S. Baxter; bowling, Messrs. R. H. Daintith, J. B. Isaac, E. Wallington and A. J. Silcock ; tennis, Mr. John Murphy.

On the pi-O-p-o-siTion—a-IVIr. ISAAC, seconded by Mr. HANDS, the meeting decided to increase the ladies' subscription from 7s. 6d. to 10s. 6d.

Mr. HANDS remarked that there was not another c.lub in England which offered the same advanages for a 7s. 6d. subscription. Votes of thanks to the chairman and officers for their past services concluded the meeting.
