SYNI

HENRY GARTONAIID, a student of sculpture in Paris, use been left a fortune of seven thousand pounds a year on condition that he is earning five hundred pounds a year bY his own labour and talent by the time he is twenty-five. If that condition is unfulfilled the money is to go to a cousin. Gastonard is now twenty-four, and there seems to be no prospect of his ever receiving the fortune. Be wr.tes to his friend Paddy O'Connell telling of his acquaintance with Mimi—" The Show Girl"—and an ad- venture with a gang of Apaches, who attack him in Paris, having designs upon a gold and diamond, cigarette-case which they think he carries, but which is actually in Mimi's possession.

To the opportune arrival of the police Henry is indebted for escaping from the ruffians with a whole skin, but he finis himself with Mimi on his hands, for the girl, who has restored to Harry the cigarette case, dares not return to her former associates. She tells him all she knows of her history, which is not much. She remembers, far back in her childhood, an old lady who was kind to her, and after that, she has no knowleige of any other life but that of a show-girl, travelling about the country with a lion-tamer, of whom she still stands in terror. At his wit's end to know what to do with his protege, Gastonard appeals to his friend Madame Lea d'Alencon.

Gastonard is convineeti that Mimi has dramatic talent, and it is decided that she shall study for a year to fit her- self for the stage. Captain d'Aleneon, husband of Madame Lea, is of opinion—quite mistakenly—that he has a cause of quarrel against Gastonard. smi challenges him to a duel. A letter to friend Paddy O'Connell brings the Irishman post haste to Paris, and he arrives to find Henry wounded and being nursed ty Mimi. It is plain to Paddy that his friend has fallen in love with Mimi, while the girl in her turn worships Gastonard. Much to the distress of Mimi, and the indignatiOn of Paddy. Madame Lea calls to see Henry, but dues not suc- ceed in her design of persuading him to return with her. Her visit, however, coupled with a belief that Henry ought to leave Paris and take steps to secure this fortune, deter- mines Mimi to leave hint, %Otte& she does secretly. In another letter to Paddy O'Connell, Gastonard tells of his search for the missing girl, with the help of a police.oftieer, amongst the people with whose like her early days had been spent.
CHAPTER X. (Continued).

[Henry Gastonard writes to Paddy O'Connell a letter concerning his search for Mimi the Simpleton.] When Farman and I were left alone in the room, no light but that of a coal fire in a broken grate, the doors closed, the silence of the wood all about us, I detected a certain un- easiness, a readiness to set his chair closer to mine and to feel for his revolver, which were some comment -upon the gallant reputation he bears in Paris. Unable to hold his tongue, he recited in low tones the story of the man Gondre, his known share in a recent story of crime, the assassinations, robberies and assaults of which the law had failed to con- vict him—and, as though this were not enough, be began to blame me for seeking Mimi at all. "She has been bred to this life," he said, "and 'nothing will wean her from it. What can you hope—to make her your mistress? Be- lieve me, she would not live with you a month. Much better to leave her to these people and return to London. If she goes with you to-night, she will leave you again. I know her kind—there are ten thousand of them in Paris, and not an honest one among them. You are risking your money, perhaps your life, in this quest. Is the girl worth it, whatever her looks?" It was difficult to answer this—for be sure the man had the logic of the argument. I could not enter upon the discussion of my reasons, ,most certainly could not coniess to him the whole truth, that I would sooner have parted with every shilling of Ty fortune than have returned to Paris without Mimi.

Happily the argument terminated before it had begun—l am quoting from you, Paddy— by the sudden appearance in the rcom of the man Gondre, the gipsy girl, and another young woman apparently of some twenty-five years of age. I have told you that there was little light to speak of. in this mean hovel. A reddening fire, a guttering candle, showed me imme- diately that the newcomer was not Mistress' Mimi nor did she resemble her in any way. To LK; candid, the girl wore an odd .and un- gainly appearance, and I had scarcely blurted out an impatient exclamation when Farman laughed aloud and asked, not altogether to my. astonishment,. "Why did you bring that boy here?" Then I perceived the truth—the so-called girl was a young actor from a neigh- bouring booth, and he still wore the clothes in which he had delighted the bumpkins of the country side.. "Why do you bring that boy here?" "Mais, monsieur, you are insulting us." "Do you wish me to remember your his- tory, Maitre Gondre? Now, comd, no non- sense. Produce the child, and we will make it worth your while." The question was direct and, demanded an answer. I realised now the dangers of our situation. These people understood that we had money upon us to ransom Mimi if she could be found. They were determined that. we should not leave the cabin with that money upon us if any wit of theirs, or vio- lence, could extort it from us. To this end the "young actor had been called from a neighbouring booth. I had no doubt that others were being summoned from other booths, and that our position must soon be- come desperate. Meanwhile, the fellow Gon- dro was protesting by the honour of all his ancestors that we had insulted him, doing what he could to detain us and showing his hand most impudently. "If this young woman is not the person you seek, lam sorry," he rejoined. "It is not my fault, monsieur. Admit that I have been ready to oblige you. I am sure the young gentleman will wish to recompense me for •my trouble. Is it not so, monsieur—you will be ready to pay us for what we have done and for any further information we can bring you? Let that be understood, and I will undertake to find the girl within a week. But naturally we are too poor to work for nothing."_

1 wa-s about to make an answer to this when Farman stood up and replied far me. I could see that the situation alarmed him, and that he was employing all his wits to extricate us from it. Agreeing apparently with the man Gondre's contention, he said that he would speak to me apart and then make them an offer. This, I think, deceived the com- pany for an instant, and before they had time to debate it, we were standing outside in the wood and the door behind us was closed.
"Run!" he said—"run—or, by God, they will murder us!"

1 did not ask him a single question, did not even care to know why a man armed with such authority as he possessed should be in danger of his life in such a place • as the woods by Rainey. It was very late by this time, and the thicket about us black, dark, and still. We took a path at hazard, and, forcing our way through the brushwood would have reached the town of Rainey itself and the railway station there, bet we had not gone fifty paces before the men were on our track, many, men, as it appeared by their shouting, and quite open in their pursuit of Us. I had a revolver with me, and I need not tell you that Farman had his, but it became clear to me that these would be of little ser- vice in such a place. When my companion pulled me from the path and dived into a thicket at the edge of a considerable copse, I would not have wagered a sovereign upon our chances, nor admitted any but tho seem- ingly inevitable conclusion to so sorry fin ad- venture.

We lay in the thicket for a couple of hours, I suppose. If the ridiculous nature of the proceeding occurred to me, be sure I was not willing to admit it. A man does many foolish things in the name of woman, but is not often ready to write about them. And I do believe, Paddy, that we came as near to being knocked on the head for fl few francs as any two men that ever set out upon a quixotic errand and forgot to count the cost of it.
Author of "The Iron Pirate " "The
Hundred Days," "A Puritan's Wife,"
etc., etc.

More than once I perceived the slouching figure of the man Gondre, as he thrashed the undergrowth and exhorted his brother ruf- fians *to 'diligence. The youth who had dis- guised himself as a girl, came into the very place where we lay, and almost stepped upon Jules Farman. This was the finest moment of it all, for, had he discovered us, Farman would have shot him dead and the rest of the gang swarmed into the copse in a mo- ment. I think he was himself afraid of the darkness and not unwilling to escape .it. When he had gone, a voice from afar called him to another covert, and we were left alone.

I should tell you, Paddy, that all th!s hap- pened at a distance, perhaps, of a couple of miles from the town. Had we run for it in the first instance, other showmen would have emerged from other booths and reinforced the gang, who would have murdered us first and robbed us afterwards as cheerfully as they would have gone to the tents to exploit the "white panther" from the Indies. For this reason, and no other, Jules Farman chose to go to ground, and I could not but admire hie prudence. When the immediate danger appeared to be abated, he led me through the wood, not toward the town of Rainey itself, but to the main eastern rail- way line, and there, by a stroke of good for- tune, we found a "merchandise" or goods train waiting At a signal cabin, and instantly boarded it and were taken to Paris. It was five in the morning when I made the Gare de FEst—an hour later when I reached my rooms in the Rue St. Paul and flung myself upon my bed as weary and disappointed a man as any in Paris. For now it is clear to me that the quest of this child is vain, and that she has deter mined to separate her lot from mine, cost her or me what it may.—Dear Paddy, yours as ever, HARRY GASTONARD.

div.head: CHAPTER XI.
div.p: CHAPTER XI.

[Hery Gastonard informs Paddy O'Connell of his probable return to London.] July 21st, 1905. Dear Paddy,—l have received your letter dated July 18th, but I cannot say that I have hastened to reply to it. This is very fit and proper, for who would dare to reply in haste to a document which contains so formidable an indictment.

I am going to the devil, you say, and go- ing, in motor parlance, upon my fourth speed. The writing is upon the wall, but 1 have no eyes to read it. A few brief months shall roll and then my inheritance pass to the amiable parson at Beldon, and I become a beggar upon the streets—or in the poor- house, is the ease may be. So be it, my dear Paddy—for what is written is written, nor shall all the tears blot out a single line. Consider the irony of it. I am to earn five hundred pounds a year by my own labours. The fortune bequeathed to me by my dear father is not to help that undertaking. Use- less for me to go into the city, to choose k Hebrew at hazard and to say to him, pay mc five hundred per annum and I will lend yoi twenty thousand. The Will forbids th: trick. The money must be earned by me, 13: my own labour and industry, or say cousii must have my fortune. Poor devil, he want. it badly. I have not .the heart to begrudge him a single penny of it. But Paddy, imagine your friend Henn Gastonard upon office stool or seeking hal; commissions in the purlieus of Throgmorton- street !Of talents I have none. I could nol earn a shilling by writing, for the news papers, or persuade even an enthusiastic friend to set up a bust of mine In any hat or cellar in Europe. The worlet has been tc me a pleasant place. I have drunk of th- fou•ntains of Bimini and quaffed draughts of perpetual youth. To dress and drive, tc dine, to dance, to sing, to sleep—behold m curriculum! I can no more imagine life with- out its music, its laughter, its love than can depict the Chatelet without its Zulema the Athenee robbed of the art of Made- moiselle Yalone. If I have lived in Paris among the Bohemians it is because they stand to me for the fullest impersonation of the joie de vivre. I may sink to poverty, pass into the shadows of obscurity—but to the degradation of the servile state, never, dear Paddy, upon my honour. So your letter leaves behind it but the gratitude of a man who bends to the truth but is obstinate to the fact. I am answerin,g it by a confession—and one which will not be very welcome to you. Yesterday I saw our old friend Lea d'Alencon again and spent many hours in her company. She is to be divorced, I understand, and Paris amused by a pretty scandal. You know how little this concerns me. You will be very sure that my meeting with her was accidental and that I forbore to seek her out of my own volition— even as I promised you. Let me say that it began with a wild din- ner given at Charine's by that mad 'volup- tuary, Willy Martin, the American. I ac- cepted his invitation because Paris has bored me very much since Mimi went away, and there are not enough decent people left in the whole city to keep a reasonable man from suicide.

We dined in a room set out to represent a cabin in the mountains. There were .back clothS of perpetual snow and cooling glaciers, distant views of mountain peaks and wonder- ful pictures of impossible valleys. The table was supposed to be. a bank of the driven snow, above which a cascade suspended its frozen waters. For .partners of the feast, there were handmaid:nig in dominoes—beau- tiful of course, because Willy Martin declared them to be so. When I drew a paper from the basin and discovered that my particular lot was to be cast with a green domino of some magnificence, then I thought of St. Patrick and of you and declared myself luck. Alas, Paddy, I had not been two minutes at the table when, despite her domino and a most excellent disguise, I dis- covered, that I had the amorous Lea for a companion and that the drawing was en- tirely to her satisfaction. It is some weeks, as you know, since I have seen this adorable creature. To judge by her conversation, she has been on the verge of a decline because of my neglect. Almost her first words destroyed that fond illusion of her poverty which ,helped her to win my sympathies when she visited me at Poissy. I no longer believe her story that d'Alen- con left her without a shilling, although it would appear to be true that hls patience is exhausted and that he is about to take a quite unusual step for a Frenchman, and to divorce her. This, if the tongue of gossip has not done her an injury (which is pos- sible), he appears to have the right to do; and yet it is delightful to hear her protest- ing her innocence and declaring that all her fault is a love of the light and a positive aversion from social darkness.

"I shall go and live in the East," she said to me in a languorous outburst, when the dinner was still young. "I must have sun- shine and music, Harry—all the sober things are hateful to me; I could 'never be an obedient wife to any man. Of course, 1 am sorry for my husband. It is the privilege of a woman 0- be sorry for the man she can- not love. He married me—l did not marry him. What child in a conveat ever marries any man, or is to be held responsible for the womanhood which comes to her afterwards. Marriage to me was a release from routine and the lives of the Saints. I had learned to hate the Saints; I would have kissed the feet of any man who closed that dreadful

book to me. And all the world was opening to my eyes, the great world, immense to the childish imagination as the heavens, and as full of golden stars. Do you wonder that I leaped for joy when they told me I was to be married."

I had never heard Lea serious before; but I do believe she was serious upon this occa- sion. My promise that if she went to the East she would hear little even of the " tom- torn " in a harem, and find the prophet's limitations trying did not move her a hairs- breadth. Had she not seen "The Belle of Teheran" as they staged it at the Bouffes, and did not that glittering spectacle of sequins and seraphs stand to her for the whole glory of the Asiatic world? "You would be one of four, Lea," I said to her, "an adorable quarter of a gloomy menage. It is true that you mould be per- mitted to sleep upon cushions, and to wash your hands in a fountain, but, my dear lady, consider the. dernier cri in turbans, and re- flect. There is no glamour of the East ex- cept in the West. Go to the Bouffes when the floats are dark, and see what the scenery looks like. Does it remind you of anything on earth which is not the apotheosis of the mean and the shabby. To me the Ea-st stands for a kind of opera comique, which is to be suffered only by those who view it from afar. I like to read of pashas and pagodas, of temple bells and little Burmese maidens; but when I am among them I think of the fleas. You, Lea, would be calling for sweet scents and a passage home before you had been in the place twenty-four hours. As for the aged Vizier who owned you, I doubt if he would have a whisker left in a week. My compassion 4ould go out to him." Well, Paddy, she refused to see it, and I perceived that for the moment some wild scheme of romance is in her head, and filmy lead her to new extravagances sufficiently wild and sufficiently foolish to astonish this Paris which loves the bizarre and the daring. She is not without rich relatives, and, as shu told me to-night, there is an uncle at Mar- seilles who is always ready to befriend her. Men are sometimes very gentle toward a woman whose chief enemy is her own beauty. Lea will find defenders, whatever may be charged against her; and it would not astonish me in the least to hear, that she had become a queen of the colony at Cairo or a novice among the Benedictine nuns at Subia- cum. Nothing, indeed, would be too out- rageous for the changing dispositions of a woman who has drunk of the cup of satiety, and already has found it bitter. Willy Martin's dinner came to an end, I should tell you, in a blaze of glory, which nearly set the restaurant on fire. A nymph, supposed to be imprisoned in the ice, but really shut up in a glass case danced a wild pas seul upon the table, and overturned the candlesticks into the lap of little Jane Merlot, from the Opera Comique. When her robe caught fire—and she could ill spare li— the soda water was employed to extinguish the flames—a bright idea, and one which set this rollicking company to other notions not less brilliant. From this moment, a battle of the corks took the place of that polite talk so dear to our forefathers.

I found myself at five o'clock of the morn- ing upon the road to Versailles in a forty- horse car driven by Lecallo, of the Opera. Lea, in a green domino, soaked to the hems in aerated waters, was at my side, and heaven alone knew whither we were going! As for Lecallo, he drove like the devil pos- sessed; and before I had quite rea.lisetj the absurdity of the venture, we stood at the 'door of the Hotel de France, at, Chartres, and a pretty crowd of early birds were cheering us to the echo.

Such, my dear Paddy, was the first stage of an adventure as ludicrous .as it was lamentable. I give you my word that would have paid a hundred sovereigns at any moment of it to have been quit of ,the pre- dicament and safely back in my own room at the Hotel St. Paul. This sum I would. have doubled when Lecallo, with intentions of the loftiest kind, chose to drive -his car on to Tours, and left me in the Hotel with one green domino and a,. crushed opera hat. Now, for a truth, was my own position both peri- lous and impossible. It became infinitely worie when Lea, disdaining all other arts. threw herself upon her genius for romance and suggested on immediate journey to r. desert island where none should discover us. "What has Paris done for us?" she asked me dramatically.

I answ(•red that it had just given us an ex- cellent dinner and a nymph in a block of ice. "Be serious, (my dear Harry," she said; "did you not tell me last night that yeii never wished to see Paris again." "Not until the morning, Lea. At night never wish to see Paris again until the morn- ing." "Ah, you jest when I am so much in earnest. Take me away, Harry, take me from all temptation—to the sea, to the woods —anywhere. if I may forget what has been, and learn to bope.•' "But, my dear Lea, does a pretty woman ever cease to hope?" "She ceases to hope when the man who should be her friend ceases to remember. I have been telling myself for the last te,n days that the luckiest day of my life was the one which detemined my husband to divorce me. The supreme injustice demands the supreme sacrifice. I am now going to blot out ten years of my life and Start again from my girlhood. I shall leave Paris, perhaps leave France. As I do not intend to deceive myself, there will be no part for religion in this ieformation of a soul. I shall live as -all the other good Women about me. Repu- tation will be nothing to me, for I shall have nothing to win by reputation. Even my name will not betray me, for T shall ly- Madame d'Alencon no more. This is my settled resolution. I am waiting to hear hu'A far you, the oldest of my friends, approve it."

This, my dear Paddy, was the astounding confession this romantic woman now • poured into my amazed ears. Whether to take it seriously, or to believe it to be the natural sequel to a night of frivolity, I know n( more than the dead.

For the moment I appetired to be con fronted by a sudden purpose, and to becom,, aware of an aftermath to the harvests folly. Lea, I said, had wearied at last o all that Paris had to give her. Love, light laughter, music—these revolted her, and sit( would turn from them. It might be pos- sible tkat the tongue of slander had wholly maligned her, and that at heart she was p, virtuous woman, seeking something as yet lacking t D her life.. Upon this I felt ablc pronounce no settled opinion. Has not ol• Georges Oleander written that the r riddle man may never solve is the riddl_ vgontar:%e confidence? "What do you want me to do, Lea?" I asked her baldly. " How can I help this

wonderful scneme or yours? vo you suggest that I buy a desert island and a camping outfit for two? Or shall it be a caravan and a month in the forests of .Amboise? You have only to say the word." Well, this pleased her immensely. . She clapped her hands at the novelty of the idea, and I could see that the "reformation of the soul" had gone to the wall for the time being, at any rate. "I should like nothing so well," she ,said. "A caravan in the forest—how absolutely delightful. Did not the Chevalier Leblanc have one last year? You remember—it was in all the papers. A motor caravan—a little bedroom, a salon, and a kitchen behind it. Mv dear Thirry. you could not suggest any- thing I would like half so well. Let us go back to Paris immediately, that I may order my dresses." "But, Lea, I don't happen to own a cara- van, and it would take some months to build one. Besides, I made no promise to .go with you—certainly not alone." She looked at me amazed. Here was a thiag that Lea d'Alencon could not for a moment understand.
"My dear Harry, what do you mean? Shall we take a sergent de rule with us, then?"

"But, Lea, consider our reputations. I grant you that this appearance at Chartres is little to our credit, tut, at the worst, we can blame the car. I don't think your friends would accept a similar excuse in the case of a caravan. We could not say that we burst a tyre and were detained for a whole month in the Forest of Amboise."

She was much piqued. Of coursv. she did not take my words literally, blt they were understood in some way as an anticipation or all she bad been leading up to, and a ready repudiation of it. Her reply intimated this in plain terms, and also was very far from that flippant response I had expected. "Are my friends' opinions anything to Me, Harry? Will they be anything when I am a divorced woman? Is it really of no concern to you whatever what happens to me after- wards? I do not believe it. Honour gives a woman claims which love may deny to her. Are you insensible to them?" "You know that I am not, Lea. My friendship for you would do much, but it would not do it upon a false compulsion of honour. The story of your life is your own. It would be no kindness to make it mine, nor should I permit you to do so." "You have never loved me, Harry." "I have often said so, Lea." "Then why do you not go away from me?" "Perhaps I shall take you at your word— in a caravan." - -
_ She laughed a little ,angrily. I cezild see that she was greatly chagrined by our brief talk, but by no means ready to accept it as final. _ _ _
"Would you leave me without a friend in Paris, Harry—must I think that of you?" "You know me better than to think it, Lea."

"But you are telling me that you mean 'to go?" "I am answering you as you asked to be answered." "And that is the man—always—always— when the flower is cut from the tree, it is &ready a dead flower to him." "Not always, Lea. I have, known him to keep it quite a long time—in a. book. But, of course, the particular man was very young. Now, here is our breakfast coming. Is not that a 'subject more agreeable to you?" She shook her head, and would not admit the fact. The repast was the dullest I have ever shared with the stately Lea, and even the purchase of a respectable frock—the best that the city of Chartres could discover—did not allay her gloom. In truth, my dear Paddy, she. has determined to marry me when her husband divorces her, and is dis- mayed to discover that I am not as deter- mined to marry her. For my part, I know not what to think, and I am woncler:ng if honour may not have something to say to me tfter all. Certain it is that her husband's jealousy chose me before others for its sub- ject, and chose me without a shred of justice or. reason. They say in Paris that there would have been a reconciliation but for that mad journey of hers to Poissy and the inn. You. Icnow how little' I was responsible for that—you do not need to be reminded of its circumstances.

All that has happened to Lea d' Alencon has been of her own seeking. For this-- rea- son my mood impels me to decline to resporid to her sentiment or to be deceived by it. Nor am I yet wholly convinced that it is real. When we returned to Paris to-night, Lecallo having called for us unexpectedly at five o'clock of the afternoon, the first decent per- son we met, upon quitting the Bois de Bou- logne, was the Count of Marcy, just returned from Dieppe, and upon his way to the En- dine. He greeted Lea rapturously, and im- mediately spoke of a little dinner at the Ritz, and of another gouple who Were to dine there with him. She accepted the invitation in- stantly, and quitted me to go and dress. It is true that I promised to meet her to-morrow and to give her a "man's opinion" upon the whole situation; but that promise will not be fulfilled. And it will not be fulfilled, Paddy, because Farman has just brought me the precious news that Mimi has been traced to England and is now engaged with a.troupe of ragamuffins playing in the barns and booths of my own country. So I go to London immediately. The de- cision- is irrevocable. And it may be that I have seen Lea d'Alencon for the last time. I will not say I wish it so, for I have called her my friend; but the event might be better in the end for her and for—Yours in great good hope, HARRY GASTONARD. (To be continued.)

-- One hundred rec,afts from Warrington o'l 29 from. Newton had a very interesting route march to, Winwick on Saturday. Major Appleton (acting adjutant/ vas in command, and the Warrington fecruits were formed int) one company under the command of the Captain of the week, captain Gordon Roberts, WI subalterns being the subaltern of the week, Lieutento" Eric Fairciough and Lieutenant Harvey Adams. The Newton men were under the direction of Sergeant' instructor Newall, and matched out from Newton ig time to meet their comrades from Warrington at Mil" wick church at 4.30 p.m. They also carried out sos3e instructive Morse signalling on the way from Newton- Sergeant-Major Ingram, the remainder of the permanent staff and every calour-sergeant from Warrington and Newton were also on parade. The Regimental Band Ids° attended and were unremitting in their excellent pler ing along nearly the whole ronte. Before marching off Major Appleton addressed 11' few words to the recruits. He said he wanted to sal' few words, especially to the recruits. While he had, been acting-adjutant during the last few days he Ii 8d watched them very easefully on parade, and be had seen much struck with their smart and soldierly appear" ance and their keenness at drill, and he considered the" a fine and well set up body of men. Before they joined this battalion they were civilians, and had the dutie° and responsibility of citizens. They were now, addition, members of one of the finest Territorial_ battalions in the Army. That battalion was part a one of the most distinguished regiments in the aol. with all Ls glorious history and traditions—the South Lancashire Regiment. In addition to their duties 1,5 citizens they had at all times to maintain the good name of their regiment which was now in their keepieg* He asked them always te be worthy of their trust' They were going, for a route march to get then, accustomed to the weight of the rifle, and in a fort,; night they h ,ped to have another march in f 0,1,1 marching order. The route taken was down Winmarleigh-street, Wilson-Patten-street, Bridge-street, Horsernarket-street, Winwick-road to Winwick (3:lurch. A halt was rue4l, at the junction of Longford-stioat and Winwick-rov, and Captain Roberti threw out an advance guard under Lieutiont Fairclough and after moving off the mail' body,Mtailed a small tear party to follow at the requisite interval under Lieutenant Adams. Cammtlei" cation vas kept with the Protective troops, and the main body by connecting files and signals were repeatedly passed from front to rear, and it was noticeable 130'd quickly the men learned the signals, which they b 3„ not yet been Wight on pirate, but many of witiott the' had nevertheless been keen enough to lest n for thew selves. After join'ng hands with their comrades fr 011: Newton the whole body grounded arms on the villa% green at Winwick, and all except the sentries over at% dispersed for 15 minutes. The fall-in was sounde shortly before five, and during the falling-in the hawe ' played for the speial benefit of the Newton men. 113;, two parties then separated and marched off, 11011e- clvered by advance and rear-guirds to their respectil- beadquartets. Before dismissing the Warrington men, MaPar Appleton said thtt the officers (including himself) been very much struck with the smartness and keens,e-i of the men dud's°.' the march, which pointed to tee that these recruits were already imbued with the eril,ll lof their battalions. THE LATE MRS. OLDFIELD.—The interment took place at the Croft Unitarian ( hapel on the 26th inst. at three o'clock, of the late Mrs. Cicily Oldtleld, who met her death at Padgate Station. The service was conducted by the Rev. J. J. Wright, F.R.S.L. Numerous friends witnessed the burial and much sorrow was expressed at her untimely end. PARISH COUNCIL AND RATEPAYERS' MEETING.—The annual meetings of the above were held in the Council School, Croft, on Monday evening. Mr. J. Ball pre- sided and there were also present —Messrs. E. W. Sankey, H. L. Southern' L. Birchen and J. W. Hunt (clerk). There was a smell attendance. The Assistant Overseer (Mr. J. W. Hunt) submitted the statement of accounts for the year and cheques were passed for payment of outstanding acoounts, leaving a balance of a 12s. Messrs. H. E. Southern and S. Welsby were re-appointed overseers and Mr. J. W. Hunt as assistant overseer and clerk to the Council. Messrs. H. E. Southern and J. Gleave were appointed burleymen.

LABOUR PARTY.-At a most enthusiastic meeting of the local Labour Party on Wednesday evening in the Wesleyan School, Mr. E. Marshall, the local secretary, gave a rousing address on the land question. The speaker fired the enthusiasm of tho comrades present and many interesting speeches were made.—Mr. George Faulknor (president) occupied the chair.

LECTITRE.—On Tuesday a well-attended lecture was delivered in the Council School, Stock-lane, by -Mks M. Brown, Poultry Lecturer for the Luicachire County Council. the subject being" Houses and housing of poultry." Miss Brown, who is a fluent speaker, gave ,a most interesting lecture which was much appreciated. Dr. Murray, J.P., occupied the chair end in thanking Miss Brown for the lecture, said how pleasea he was to see so many present.

WESLEY GU IL 13.—The closing social of the Wesley Guild was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Satur- diy availing, Mrs. James Dodds presiding. The social was opened with a first-class musical programme which consisted of pianoforte solos, vocal solos and duets, recitations, Scc. The artistes were : The Misses Moores, Walters, Poster, and Bates; Messrs. Tegg, Phcenix and Kay. Miss Johnson ably performed the duties of accompanist. The concert over, refreshments were banded round and ,then gimes followed. What was unanimously voted a very enjoyable evening vtas brought to a close with a short dance. '

ELOCUTIONA RY RECITA t.—Elocution is undoubtedly an art, and one of its ablest exponents is Mr. Joseph S. Hodgson, who gave bis fourth elocutionary recital at the Friends School on Monday. evening. An excellent programme was given, and each item was applauded most enthusiastically. The items were as follows : "The Pied Piper of Namelin " (Browning); "The Just Judge" (a tale of Sir Matthetv Hale) ; Etiquette, "Bab Ballads" (W. S. Gilbert) ; "The Painter of Seville" (Susan Wilson); "Hiawatha's Photograph- ing" (Lewis Carroll) ; "It mud ha been war" (York- shire Dialect) ; Scene from "The Rivals " (Sheridan.; " Mrs. Alalaprop," (Miss Oddie) ; " Lydia Languish " (Miss Marsland) ; "Sir Anthony Absolute" (T. S. Hodgson.) —Mr.Brown presided over a good attendance. —Votes of thanks to Mr. Hodgson and the Chairman were proposed and seconded by the scholars.

div.head: PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: PARISH COUNCIL.

That much discussed question, of the nightsoil con- tract, was up again at the meeting of the Sankey Parish Conncil held last Monday evening in the Sankey Council School. Mr. W. Taylor presided and he was assisted in his'deliberations by Messrs. W. Furness, J. W. Walters, W. H. Ireland, W. Ditchfield, ll.'Fair- dough and J. Smith (clerk). Mr. Fairciough opened by saying he thought that the cost of the nightsoil should be as it was, and not put on the rates, but Mr. Furness explained that Mr. Whit- field would only carry a certain portion, and he asked whether a man could be got to take Mr. Whitfield's leavings. Continuing be said the matter was not within the province of the District Council, as yet, so if a gentleman could be got there would be no further difficulty in the matter. This would not do for Mr. Walters who claimed that the property owners were very dissatisfied about it. Mr. Fairclough then maintained that the work was done Satisfactorily.
Mr. Walters was very emphatic when he replied that it was not done satisfactoi ily. Mr. Pairclough then disclosed the information that the Inspector had told him that the work had been done properly.

Mr. Walters, however, contended that the ratepayers were not satisfied. Continuing he said he had had several of them complaining to him and they thought that it was time that the contract went upon the rates. _ At this point Mr. Ireland rose to confirm what Mr. Fairelough had said, and the work had been done as satisfactorily as it any other district in the rural dis- trict of Warrington. Mr. Furness said that did not touch the question at all. The question was whether a man could be found to take Mr. Whitfield's leavings. Cont:nuing he said Distant Council could not move in the matter, but if they were to ta.ke the responsibility they would have to levy a rate for the purpose of having it collected. If that Council approached the District Council they must eo so as a public body, who would be bound to put a rate on. Fairclough maintained that there was no necessity for the charge to go on the rates. What Mr. Whitfield would not do another man would, and he did not think the time was ripe for such a step. Mr. Walters: I think the time is quite ripe. Con- tinuing he said that if a rate were levied the balance of the wodey could be used for the purpose of laving more lighting, for it was very bad indeed in same parts of Sankey. It was the farmers who did not want the co'ntract to go on the rates.—Eventually the discussion was postponed until next Monday evening, when it is hoped that a satisfactory conclusion wall be arrived at.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY PARISH MEETING.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY PARISH MEETING.

The parishioners of Great Sankey met on Monday evening to discuss affairs relating to their parish. Mr. William Taylor presided and he was supported by Mr. J. Smith (clerk). There was a fair attendance and immediately the meeting had been opened Mr. Randall wanted to know what the District Council were doing with regard to the. night soil. Mr. FurnesS explained that the District Council were not in a position to collect the nightsoil, and therefore the Council could not levy a rate for that purpose. Mr. A. Tongs proposed : "That this Council take the matter up andlhat the nightloil be removed by the District Council."

Ihi-; was seconded by Mr. C. E. Bromley. At this juncture a further explanation to that of Mr Furne:s was forthcoming from Mr. Trehind who said that Mr. Fairclough had been able to find a man who would treat the matter successfully. Continuing, he said there would be another Meeting of the Parish Council on Monday evening to go into the matter further.
Mr. Haley thought that there was no serious reason to complain of how the work was being done at the present time. _ _ _
Mr. Fairelough moved an amendment that the matter be left as it was.
Mr.Unsworth seconded and it was carried by 11 to 4.
THE GARDEN SUBURB.

Mr. Randall desired to know whether the expense of a special rate was to be borne by the ratepayers for the sewer that bad been put down at the Garden Suburb. Mr. Furness said that would come as a special rate. It would cost £25 to £3O. It would come on the next half-year which would beg;n on the Ist of April. Mr. Haley said that in regard to the levying of that rate he understood that such a rate would fall upon the property owners to the fullest extent, but so far as the landlord was concerned it would ouly fall on him at the rate of one-fourth. Mr. Farness observed that the new houses would have to pay a portion. The Clerk : We shall have to levy a special rate for the half-year. In the next half-year, the District Council will pay the lamp lighting rate, and combine that with the cost of the sewer, making a special rate, and then ultimately the lamp lighting rate will come back to whoTe it was before. Continuing, be said that the farm land and buildings came to one-third of the total valuation of the township.

THE PRICE OF GAS. • Mr. Randall desired to know whether they were going to have a reduction in gas: Mr. Furness said that the matter was brought before the Parish Council some few months ago, and they recognised that they had beau treated very unfairly by the Warrington Corporation. No les3 than three reductions had been made in the Borough on the price of as to consumers, and; it appeared to them, al a Parish Council, unfair that Sankey should pay the same rates. They had taken steps with a view to bringing pressure on the Borough with the object of getting a reduction. They had been trying to draw in other parishes with a view to getting a formidable committee' to show them the unfairness with which they were heinE treated. Mr. Randall moved "That this Parish meetinglof Great Sankey desires to respectfully draw the atten- tion of the Warrington Corporation Gas Committee to the charge wade for gas, considering that several reductions have been to customers within the Borough and no concession has been made to this • Parish for public lighting." Mr. Tongs seconded and the resolution was carried unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. Furness seconded by Mr Ut:sworth a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman.

MAY QUEEN.—The work in connection with the festival is well in hand. It has been decided to hold the festival on the football field as in previous years. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.—Anniversary services in. connection with this Church were held on Sunday last. The pastor occupied the pulpit in the morning, and the Rev. A, Goodrich, D.D., of Alanebester, in the evening. In the afternoon a children's service wbs held, when an address was given by the Rey. A. Barrett. On Tuesday the annual church social was held when reports for the past year were given, and a statement of the result of the bazaar recently held was presented, which showed a balance after pa} ing all expenses of about £203.

INDEPENDFNT METHODIST CHURCH.—A tea meeting , and concert was held on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. Hardy Holt occupied the chair at the concert, and in ! the course of his opening remarks dwelt upon the ser- vice done by the small country churches to the large cities, and emphasized the importance of the work amongst the young.—Mr. William Mort also addresQed the meeting, recalling same amusing reminiscences of his boyhood days in connection with this church which delighted and enter timed the audience. Mr. Richard Hewitt gave a financial report in which he referred to the special effort which w.rs being made to reduce the debt incurred • when the Wilding was altered and enlarged. Miss Mary Brundrett of Lymm, Miss Clarke of Warrington, and Mr. Hughes of Warrington rendered solos and Miss Ethel Moston of, Lymm recited. Mr. Atkinson of Warrington accompanied. A LYMM TRADESMAN'S CLAIM.—At the Salford Hundred Court of Record, on Thursday, before His Honor Judge Roskill, K.C., George William Cross of Bridgewater-street, Lymm, Painter and Decorator, sued William Kirkpatrict of the Bridgewater Arms, Lymm, for £9 Is. for work done on a sub-contract at Lynom.— Mr. Rushton (instructed by Mr. G. L. Welford, solicitor of Manchester and Lymm) represented the plaintiff,and Mr. T. B. Leigh (instructed by Messrs. Arthur Browne and Co., Solicitors,Warrington) appeared for the defend- ant. Two defences were pleaded, first to the jurisdiction of the Court as it_was alleged that all the transactions took place at Lymm outside the jurisdiction, and secondly, the debt was not due until the defendant had received cheque for the full contract which was to be on the 30th November last, and that pro- ceedings had been commenced long before that date. It was also stated during the case that the defendants solicitors had offered to pay the debt when it became due, but such offer was refused. After hearing lengthy arguments by Mr. Rushton and Mr. Leigh on the point of jurisdiction, his Honour held that he had no Juris- diction as the whole transaction took place at Lymm, and therefore gave judgment for the defendant with costs.

WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.—A public meeting in support of-this movement was held on Friday last in the Drill Hall. HEAVY PENALTIES ON FOWL .STEALERS.—Jam es Occleston and Joseph Whitfield, Loth of Caditlead, were ch irgei on Tuesday with stealing born the Mersey Farm, Partington, between 7 p.m. on Saturday March 29th, and 7.30 the next morning, ten fowls, the property of Leonard Rodgers. They pleaded guilty.— Detective Inspector Pierce, stationed at Altrincham proved the casa.--Tbe Chairman said that Occleston was a bad character in every tense of the word. They wore determined to put. a stop to this. fowl stealieg. Occleston would have to go to goal for six months with bard labour and Whitfield for four months with hard labour.

A SEAMAN'S ALLEGED THEFT.—A middle-aged ' man, named Frederick Wilkinson, Burslem, was charged with stealing on August 3rd. 1907, from the ship Burrancer, whilst at Partington Wharf, two gold watches, a silver chain, a gold ring and a quantity of Danish and Swedish money, of the total value of £l2 Is. 6d., the property of Charles Alson.—Prisnner said he wented legal advlee.Whether he was dealt with there or sent for trial, he would not plead guilty.—He was remanded for eight days, and the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Harris) informed him that he must tell the Gpvernar at Knuts- ford tliat he wanted legal advice.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
SUICIDE OF A RUNCORN BOATMAN.

At the inquest at Altrincham on Monday concerning the death of Richard Creswell, aged fifty-two, briatman, Runcorn, ho was found hanging in the canal stables at Broadheath on Saturday morning, it was stated that deceased on Friday had appeared upset about his hor:e's shoulders, which were a bit sore, and was afraid of being stopped. His father also said that about a week ago he was fined for not sending his children to school. He did not pay the fine, and so the police took him from his boat, and this preyed on his mind. It was also explained that the deceased's horse was hired, and did not belong to the boat. A verdict of" Suicide whilst temporarily insane, was returned."

div.head: FATAL FALL IN WIDNES HOTEL.
div.p: FATAL FALL IN WIDNES HOTEL.

"Accidental death "was the verdict at the coroner's inquiry at Widnes on Saturcay. into the ceath of Leonard Herriman (46), a mineral water carter, residing at 45, Witt-rcad, whose death took place on Wednesday- From the evidence it, appeared that. on Saturday week Herriman slipped and fell in the lobby cf the Alexandra Hotel Midst d elivering an order, and fractured two Loues of the left leg above the ankle.—Dr. Lindsay, who stated that the deceased developed delirium tremen said it was not always the measure of the actual amount of drink ta ien that brought on delirium tremens. It might be set up in a moderate drinker who received an injury. It was not suggested that Heirirtaa was an - thing but a moderate drinker.

The Clerk reported that at a meeting of the Is.llation Hospital Committee the resignation of Miss J. Davies, matron of the Hospital, was tendered and accepted and it mas decided to advertise for a matron at a salary of £4O per annum with ap.attrnents, rations, and washing.

Mr. Woodward moved that Dr. Adams be reappointed medical officer of health for the District Council for the ensuing year at a salary of £l5O per annum. This was seconded and carried.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
NATIONAL UNION OF LABOUR.

On Satm day night the third annual reunion of the members of the four St.Helens branches of the National Amalgamated Union of Labour was held at the Co-operative Hall. Over 500 were present. Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., presided at the tea, but Mr. Glover,M.P., and Mr. J. N. Bell, general secretary, were prevented from attending. The arrangements were in the hands of Mr. T. Williamson, official delegate, and the event was most successful. MOTORISTS FINED AT ST. HELENS.

At St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a charge of driving a motor-car to the danger of the publics was down for bearing against Henry Beecham, of Huyton, but Mr. E. W. Swift, who appeared for the defence, said he believed the police.would be content to alter the charge to one of exceeding the speed limit. If that were done Mr. Beecham would plead guilty. The Chief Constable agreed. It was stated that at noon on Thursday, the 18th inst., defendant was driving a motor-car from St. Helens in the direction of Prescot. Between the Bird-in-Hand and Toll Bar the car was driven at quite thirty miles an hour. Mr. Swift said that when spoken to by the police Mr. Beecham at once admitted that be had been travelling more than twenty miles an hour, and the only excuse be asked him to offer was that it was raining at the time and that he was making his way to Huyton for lunch. The Bench imposed a fine of £3 and £1 9s. costs. THE LATE MR. E. CANNINGTON,

A touching tribute of respect to the memory of the late Mr. E. CAnnington, J.P., Wa S evidenced on Sunday eveningin the Central Hall, Renshaw-street, Liverpool, by the presence of 2,000 persons who took part in the memorial service. The front of the r latform was draped in black, with a beautiful floral gift. Amongst those on the platform were the Revs. Joseph Jackson, T. Galland Hartley, and Mr. and „Mrs. Gipsy Evans.

The Rev. T. Galland Hartley delivered an eloquent address, in which he remarked that one of their noblest and best had been taken from them daring the past week. It was his privilego to know that Mr. Cannington during his ministry at Waterloo. He was a man of broad sympathies, awl, therefore, a lover of God, and everything that tended towards the good of minkind generally. Godliness was the socrat of his successful fe and service, which showed itself in the fidelity and maintenance of everything that was good and great. The supreme question with which he (the preqcher) closed was, how minv out of that great gather.ng would be baptised for the dead. There was a gap open in their ranks, and they wanted that vacant position filling up. He therefore asked them to go forward and still win victories for Christ.

div.head: WARRINGTON PIIILOMATHIC SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON PIIILOMATHIC SOCIETY.
M. George Jennison on the " Taxation of Land Values."

A meeting of the above Society was held on Wednes- day at Gregory's Cafe, when Mr. George Jennison, of the 95 Club, Manchester, delivered a lengthy and interesting address upon "The Taxation of Land Values." In the course of his remarks Mr. JENNISON said that the land was everything. Taxation of Land Values meant the taxation of land cn its natural unimproved value arising from site or fertility. This taxation would at once reduce unemployment and would soon prevent all poverty from unemployment without i interfering n any way with the natural sur- plus of labour which is necessary to the development of industry. It would also be sufficient to pay all taxes. These things it would accomplish by free access to the soil. The tax would make it uneconomical to hold land unused, and in this way, if the tax were 20s. or say 19s. in the it would put everyone on equal ground, for rent is the difference between the best awl worst land, and this would be paid to-the State. ,The tax on land values marked the altera- tion from failure to pfogress. Such progress was con- tinuous. Its example was contagious, and its staccess admitted by opponents. In New South Wales land- owners who were supposed to be the greatest sufferers, would not change it. The general improvement was so good ti at it counterbalanced even their loss. The benefit of the tax was speedily felt in Germany. The taxation of Lind va)ues would be as valuable in England as in these sparse colonies. While land could be held speculatively there would also be a large number on the margin of subsistenca. Men held on and would take anything rather than st:lrve. Were he a Tory it would be to the law of 1632 he would appeal and boldly ask once again for 4s. in the But without, calling on the past there was a good case for the Chan- cellor who wanted an extra £20,000,000 to raise it by a id. on land. The laud of England was valuable from the efforts of the people of England and he scouted the idea of-any robbery in taxing it. Its value was easily ascertained and itself immovable, appeals would diminish and evasion become a falling art. lie appealed to the three great parties for support in a tax on land values, to the Socialist because it went part of the way that he would -tread : to the Protectionist because it would mitigate their sufferings if they had the misfortune to succeed, but chiefly to the Free Trader. To him he would say " Free the land : complete the great work os Cobden and ,carry forward to its finish that scheme of freedom which Cobden was obliged to leave half done. Then indeed would freedcm stand revealed. No longer should the mocker, taunting our wealth, point the finger at the squalid poverty and misery which disgraced our nation. But everywhere each citizen should enjoy to the full the fruit of his labour and the countries of the world should serve him freely. None need be poor: none need be servile: to each should be a life of freedom and with freedom—Peace." (Loud applause)._

nMr. E:GORDON BURGESS and Mr. JAMES BALL res- pectively proposed 4.nd seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Jennison, and incidentally criticised his proposals. —The vote was carried with acclammation, and Mr. JENNISON, in thanking the meeting,- replied to the criticisms put forward.

div.p: Walking Day Festival.

Sir, —Seeing the above annual Sabbath School treat is fast approaching, could I through the medium of your paper, persuade the Free Church Council and Nonconformists generally to arrange to join in the procession. The public appreciation of Sabbath School work is shown by the thousands who line the route. Parents and friends from neighbouring towns ilock in to see the attractions of the Church and Catholics who turn out in full strength. It is really surprising that only Buckley-street Methodist Mission Ragged School Mission, and the Salvation Army represent the other section. Surely the time honoured custom of our town is worthy of maintaining by a united display.—Yours,
INTERESTED.

div.head: -- The Particular Baptists.
div.p: -- The Particular Baptists.

Sir,—May Ibe allowed to give in your columns a little of the history of the Particular Baptists in Warrington, as there has been a rather:rmsleading account by the Golborne-street Bazaar Handbook. The Particular Baptists first commenced to have meetings in Warrington about 1819, but, on January 23rd, 1826, they formed a Church, meeting at a place in Buck's-yard, Bridge-street. They were members from Hill Cliffe who had tired of the disturbances that were occurring in that church. They remained in Buck's-yard fill they removed to Dallam-lane, in 1833, as I find a letter from the Bishop of Chester recog- nising it as a Protestant Church. In the year, 1848, September 3rd, ths first move was made to build a chapel in a healthier spot, so they built one in Bewsey- street which was opened on September 27th, 1849. The Particular Baptists occupied this place till 1869, when the Cheshire Rines Railway bought it as it was on the line of their railway route. But this Church did miet die out at Bewsey-street as anyone would think by reading the history just published. Another Chapel was erected in Legh-street, called by the same name, Ebenezer Particular Baptist Chapel, to which the Church was transferred, and it was opened in January 1871, where it now stands, the same doctrines still being taught in that place at the present day where the One true and Holy God is worshipped. As to their remarks about our people verging on to Antinomianism I leave that for others to judge who know the true tenets of our teachings. The above is a true account, taken from books, with the record of all our Church business that we have in our possession, not one word from hearsay. 162, Padgate-lane, Warrington
JOHN L. BATE

Efficiency and Employment. have followed the discussion between Mr Parker arid Labor Omnia Vincit with some interest, and am pleased to note that the former has abandoned his satire, and lifted the debate to a serious plane. The economics of Mr. Parker as evinced in his letter are mostly sound, but I think that an effort should be made to get him to look a little deeper, and a little farther than his vision has so far carried him. I entirely agree with him that labour is not a fixed limited quantity—the wage fund theory is an exploded one— and I believe that it is worse than futile to try to provide increased employment by protective tariffs, as these would divert labour from where it is more productive, into industries where it would be less productive. . The aim of economists should be, not to provide more work, but to increase production, not forgetting, however, that production is only a means, not an end. And it does not necessarily follow that more work would mean increased production. Wealth is not determined by the amount of labour, but by what labour produces. The more efficient labour is, the greater is the wealth produced, and as the demand for employment comes from the National Dividend (or, the net national product), the greater the wealth produced, the greater the demand for the agents of production. Efficiency therefore cannot increase unemployment. Whilst we so far agree, a pint of difference seems to appear when Mr. Pat ker asserts that any economy in production through competition is handed down to the consumer. A difficulty arises here. It is not clear whether Mr. Parker means that the whole benefit of the lessened cost of production goe's to the con- sumer. If he means this, then his statement that "if by the introduction of a machine the saving were only sufficient to balance the saving of labour, the machine would not be employed, because there would be no benefit," is apparently contradictory. Assuming, however, that he contends that the whole benefit goes to-the consumer, I join issue with him on the point. According to Alfred Marshall, professor of Political Economy in the University of Cambridge, " seme who are called artisans, together with many unskilled labourers, are unable to obtain for them- selves or their children, the means of living a life that is worthy of man." If Mr. Parker's contention is correct, what is his explanation of the fact that so many people are com- pelled to live on the border line of poverty? All other • things being equal, I admit that in time, cheapened production would eliminate poverty. But I suggest that the fact that undeserved poverty is so -Prevalent, despite the greater efficiency of the worker, and the larger utilization of natural forcf s, proves that the consumer does not receive all the benefit, and suggests a factor somewhere which operates against the general diffusion of the advantage of cheapened production. , The factor of economic freedom, as competition has been called, which operates in the case of the capitalist-producer to modify the results of lesser expense of production, also operates, with greater force, in the case of the worker's wages, and thus affects his power of demand as a consumer. I say "with greater force," for in the case of the worker, the free play of competitive forces is only modified by Iris organisation, whereas in addition to more effective organisation and greater reserve force, the capitalist- producer has the dominating advantage of owning the instruments of production. There is no equality of terms in bargaining between employer and employS,the latter being under the disadvantage of having nothing to sell except his labour, which he must sell or starve. And here we come to the cause of the error of dis- tribution, which results in such inequality, and which disproves Mr. Parker's assertion that the consumer receives- the benefit of cheaper production. The operation of economic law is interfered with by an antagonism of interests and waste, which are occasioned by private competing capitals. The factors that prevent the enjoyment by all of the benefits of improved industrial arts sh( uld be eliminated, and I would invite Mr. Parker to suggest a method that would effect this, short of an adjustment of industrial relations, that would make production a. regulated social function.
DEMOCRAT.

Sin—Your correspondent Labor Omnia for the third time in almost identical words asserts that the consumer will not benefit by efficiency due tb temperance, or anything else, as long as the means of production are owned and controlled for the benefit of the few. gay I remind him that the repeated assertion of a belief does not make it true. Our Iriend appears to be so obsessed by his one idea that it seems to blot out everything else or at least dis- tort its proportions. It is difficult to think how even one so possessed can show how when an article is cheapened, say by efficient machit.ery, that those who buy, the consumers, are not benefited if-they can get -what they want-for less money, and yet this is what Labor Omnia Vincit. asserts. He fnust attach to the word " benefit " some peculiar meaning of his own. In the industries most benefited by .efficiency not only are the products most reduced in cost, thus benefiting the consumer, but the wages in these indus- tries have risen most, and yet our friend contends there is no benefit to the working producer, and the working consumer. In those countries where efficiency has developed most, wages in all grades are highest,

for example in America and England; and conversely wages are lowest in those countries and industries where there is the least efficiency, least machinery, least applied science, and least human capacity—in such the worker's share has advanced least. , Using Mr. Bowley's calculation in his "Wages in the United Kingdom" and Sauerbeck's index number for the price of commodities, we find wlth Professor Chapman that the advance in real wages, not nominal, in the half century ending 1900 was 50 per cent. Some authorities say 60. But inasmuch as Sauerbeck does not include rent, which is one of the few things which has become dearer during the period in ques- tion, we may accept 40 per cent. advance as a very

safe figure. Inasmuch as Labor Omnia Vincit states that "half the present population do not get sufficient to keep them in a state of physical efficiency" if the 40 per cent. increase were taken off then what would be his figure for the underfed? This is another of our friend's statements for which he proffers no proof. Nothing damages a cause so much as exaggeratton, and by it your correspondent discredits the one he would help. But he may contend the advance has not been uniform, that while in some trades wages may be nearly doubled, in others the advance has been little. This .is so, and if the fact ,be examined it will further confirm my con- tention that efficiency benefits the workers. Are not the trades, taken as a whole (as I have already shown) which have advanced most in efficiency the ones in which wages have risen most,and is not labour worst paid in the occupations which have developed least and which do not lend themselves to the aid of machinery, applied science, etc.? Labour Omnia Vincit may say it is little comfort to the farm labourer who gets 12s. (if farm labourers get only this, which I doubt) that an engineer gets three times the amount. Where the downward social pressure is felt most is amongst the unskilled. Manual labour has relatively, but not actually, beeome less valuable, and the problem of to-day is our responsibility as individuals and as a State to the inefficient who form _ .

the bulk of the unemployed and unemployable. Since writing the above, through the courtesy of the Editor, I have received an advanced copy of an admirable letter, signed " Democrat," which was sent for insertion in last week's " Examiner." I agree with almost every word in this letter, and am obliged to "Democrat" for his admirable presentation of my case in his second paragraph. He must not forget, however, that the primary contention with Labor Omina Vincit was in respect to the effect of intemperance on unemployment, and in regard to this distinctly limited issue I gather that in this we agree. I did not say, nor did I mean to imply, that the whole benefit of the lessened cost of produc- tion, say through temperance, goes to either the pro- ducer or the consumer. Sufficient for my limited purpose was to prove that the producer and consumer does benefit, which Labor Onmia Vincit denies. The further point about the whole benefit introduces us into a phase of the subject which is much more complicated, and if followed out would lengthen this correspondence very much. I quite agree that there is a factor which operates against the general diffusion of ' benefit due to cheapened production. In other words that the advantage before it comes to the proper quarter is subject to a discount (which may be con- siderable) but it is after all only a discount, be it large or small, upon the whole, not the whole itself as Labor Omnia Vincit seems to think. I am quite with Democrat when he says the factors that prevent the enjoyment by all [workers] of the benefits of improved industrial arts should he eliminated. Probably Democrat and myself would differ as to the factors which prevent this general enjoyment, but the whole tone of his letter and the grasp he manifests of the question would lead me to hope that if We did not ultimately agree we should at least be able to reduce our differences to a very small compass. I appreciate any effort to make m 9, look deeper and farther than lily vision has so far carried me," but I am not sure if Democrat quite appreciates how for I see, and this is natural in view of the limited aspect of the question raised by Labor Omnia Vincit about intemperance, to which I have tried to confine the issue and to avoid wandering into regions in which the Problems become more intricate.
CHARLES E. PARKER Penketh, March 31st, 1909.

Mr. Gray and National Service. Sir, The whole of Mr. Gray's articles are full of admirable sentiment, but very one-sided reasoning. .The pith of his argument lies in those last sentences in his final reply to Mr. Townrce, viz. : ' "It is not a question to me of Mr. Haldane's cal- culations, or 8 Dreadnought's, etc. etc.,but whether the respective democracies have commonsense enough to see the futility of War, but the issues rest. with the people, were they wise enough to £OO them."

Good heavens, what a great discovery? The same thoughts were expressed by others long ago, and are held to-day-by all right thinking and sane men. 'Fite great point Mr. Gray has entirely overlooked, is that this great idea to federate Europe, can only be accom- plished when the people of the whole of Europe are ready for it. Time alone will undoubtedly accomplish this, but when, no man can tell. He goes on to sty—" This War God is enthroned by small rival sections only, etc. etc.,"—' and that behind the National Service League there is an ultet ior political object.' I differ with him most strongly ; I beg to point out to him that the chief object of the N.S.L.,— which includes in its ranks all shades of opinion—is to enable a man to be fit and ready to defend his country should war be ever forced upon us, and not to clamour for it. He asks Mr. 'Pnwnroe, " Where is the semblence of a quarrel, betwixt the people of Germany and our- selves ?" There are many reasons that a student of history will readily see. The Germans 'are in a similar position to the Japanese before their con- flict with Russia ; the cause of that strife was expan- sion. Germany has the same reasons and aims, but with this addition, her shipping and commerce have increased enormously, and are still increasing. They want coaling stations of their own, and know that they cannot get them for the simple reason that all that is worth having, we hold. "Any semblance of a quarrel, etc ?" Whoever dreamed that in 'B4 she would be at war with and beat Austria and in '67, who thought that three years hence the Germans wuuld be in Paris. As one famous writer so clearly puts it : "There is no sense whatever in regarding other nations with suspicion, or in doubting that they are as desirous of peace as ourselves. There is no more peace-loving or domestic people in the world than the Germans. Yet in a lifetime, they have been at war with three neighbours, the Danes, Austrians and the French."

Was there any sign of quarrel in 1817 with the French, as I have stated, "No!" Yet it is a known fact, that Germany was quietly, and determinedly preparing, and only struck when absolutely ready. Is Mr. Gray prepared to deny that it was a manu- factured and unjust quarrel? I am no Jingoist Heaven forbid, but in the face of the enormous developments at the Ktupp works, and elsewhere, their quiet bulldog determination over their navy, a F ecrecy exactly as in '6B, it behoves as to prepare with the same determination, to the utmost that lies in cur power. If we were sure of the sincerity of these people, I -would unhesitatingly endorse all that Mr. Gray has had to say. But we are not sure. His fourth question is What good would accrue-- if this cpuntry fought and beat Germany ? My answer is none But the great point is, what would Germany gain if she fcught and beat us? Therein, I claim is the whole secret, if secret it be, of the existence of this great national movement, to be pre- pared should war be ever forced upon us. In the face of facts there is but one issue, the formation of an adequate home defence, a defence with no shirkers, which would I am confident abate this fierce race between the two. The one thing that is an induce- ment to others to attack us is the weakness behind the navy. I submit that the fact —if the N.S.L. pro- posals came in force the knowledge that every man would have to take his share in home defence, wculd tend to modify that rashness of opinion and jingoism, that springs up in time of trouble, and would be a guarantee of peace. —Yours truly, 10, Monks-street.
THOITAS -WILLIAMS.

div.head: "IMPROVEMENTS IN EXISTING TOWNS."
div.p: "IMPROVEMENTS IN EXISTING TOWNS."
Alderman Bennett and the Allotment
Holders.

While garden suburbs are eminently desirable and indeed necessary as an outlet for the teeming popula- tions of our busy towns, too much importance cannot be attached to the improvement of the towns themselves, where the msjority of the working people are com- pelled to spend their lives. This phase of a commend- able movement is receiving special attention from the Beautiful Warrington Society and on Thursday evening the members were favoured with a visit from Mr. George Rose, chairman of the Liverpool Garden City Association, who gave an address in the Museum Lecture Room on " Improvements in Existing Towns." Mr. Rose is a thorough enthusiast in the work, his ideals are high, and he has the gift of expressing them in an attractive and telling style. His lecture was interest- ing throughout and full of useful suggestions. He pointel out that in most if not in all of our large towns there was much that was beautiful an 4 worth preserving and opportunities of improvement were constantly occurring. Having referred to the want of foresight which had been exhibited in the past, Mr. Rose said it had been steted that Liverpool might have been made one of the most beautiful cities in Europe. Dis- onesing the lines on which improvements should pro- ceed, Mr. Rose said a good idea was to get a map of the town, colour green all the parks, gardens and open spaces, and see where and how a wide boulevard° could be laid :out Eto girdle the town. Such a boulevarde should :1 (as close in to the centre of the town and as wide as possible, and should endeavour to take in every natural adv outage, such as groups of trees, a flowing stream and some fine point of view. Lateral or radial cross streets would suggest themselves as districts were obened, up. Of course such a scheme sounded easier than it proved in practice. If it became known that a boulevard was contemplated the land went up in price and it was therefore a matter for careful arrangement. The lecturer touched upon the" unholy conglomeration " of crowded dwellings in the Owns and said the wretched squalid rookeries would never have been allowed, but for want of thought and absence of the right public sentiment. Indifference amounting almost to mental blindoese was the canker that seemed to be eating at the hart of the nation. He suggested that authorities should limit the erection of Cottage property to so many per acre and that when they undertook the housing of the people the dwellings should be such as to assist the inhabitants to develop a higher standard of life. Baths should be provided in at least the larger and higher-priced tenements. Every town authority should have power to prevent the destruction of trees and shrubs and even without that power very much might be done by negotiations with builders or land owners when a new building arca was started upon. Mr. Rose urged the provision of Islay- grounds for every group of cottage property, and the holding of " arbor days," and the instruction of school children as to the names of trees. In the streets of Washington the trees numbered 80,000 and in Paris there were about 100,000, over £lo,oto a year being spent on trees alone. Why could ,it not to arranged that when buildings were demolished and the area was not to be immediately built upon, the land should be cleared and planted. In this connection Mr. Rose suggested that the vacant land near the Warring- ton County Court might be planted with trees at a small expense. The clearing and planting of vacant lands—at present often wildernesses of brickbats and unsightly rubbish heaps—would provide work for a large number of unemployed. It was really distressing to see so many of the larger houses in Northern towns, with their fine gardens, shut off with high brick or stone walls—surely the acme of brutal selfishness! Other improvements advocated by the lecturer were the cultivation of creepers, the planting of railway banks and approaches with tress, the mitigation of the smoke nuisance—in which connection be alluded to the eminent example of Messrs. Crosfield who computed that they had saved about £25,000 by the adoption of up-to-date methods of dealing with smoke—and the provision for the workers of counter-attractions to the public-house. He was also strong in his condetenstion of the "athertisement fiend" and his unsightly hoardings and incidentally mentioned that the Liverpool Corporation had sacrificed 0,000 by not allowing the electric trams to be disfigured with advertisements. 1 hose who desired the City Beadtiful would also have to wage perpetual warfare on the noises of the streets. With the, electric tram and the harsh hoot of the motor, what lenguagewas too strong? The Rev. Canon STaveesoe, who presided, said that althouth they mot with diecouragements and could wish to see a very much greater interest kindled in this matter amongst the populations of our great towns, he for one had never lost his faith that the movement was going to grow and that we were at the beginning of changes which would be groat, beneficial and far-- reaching. He proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer. Alderman Bazetrry, in seconding, had some aliting remarks to make as to the apathy and indifference on thequestion. He saidhe was a great believer in allot- ments and he was delighted when the Town Council set apart a portion of Victoria Park for that purpose. But he began to wonder whether the allotments were not a miseake when after the tenants had been in occupation for a few months, they sent a petition asking the Coun- cil either to drastically lop or cut down entirely some of the most beautiful trees in the town which happened to border on the allotments. He would rather do with., out the tenants and allotments than cut down the trees. The destruction of old houses was a standing difficulty we had to face in Warrington and other towns. It almost broke . his heart to see the absolute want of feeling and sentiment which characterised so many of his fellow townspeople. Where destruction was inevitable the new buildines should be so erect &las to recall old associations, and he was glad that one of the local firms of brewers contemplated that course in regard to the demolition of a picturesque old house in Warrington. Alderman Bennett waxed indignant at the "fatuous blindness and idiotic stupidity" which was being manifested with regard to the Knutsford-road improvernent.For the mere a.ke of redwing the rates to some extent the Council were allowing houses to be re-erected on the narrow strip of land between Knutsford-road and the river, which could not possibly comply with the byelaws. The prospect of the bridge improvement would therefore be spoiled by the vista of backyards which an enlightened Corporation pro- posed to inflict on posterity rather than sacrifice this piece of land. Alderman Bennett 'concluded by urgine the workpeople of Warrington to avail themselves of the garden suburbs and expressing the hope that Mr. John Burns' Bill to give municipalities greater power in dealing with improvements would become law. The vote was heartily accorded and a similar com- pliment was paid to the Chairman on the motion of Mr LONGLA.ND, seconded by Mr. ROSE.
