div.head: Runaway Horse.
div.p: Runaway Horse.

At noon on Wednesday a horse attached to a van belonging to Messrs. Bennett, confectioners, Lovely- lane, took fright near Warrington Bridge and dashed towards Market Gate. Many futile attempts were made to check its career, but it was eventually br3ught to a standstill by Thomas Headley, employed by Mr. Gill, butcher, Buttermarket-street, who pluckily seized it by the head. The street was very busy with traffic at the time and it was fortunate that no-one was injured.

div.head: MOTOR CARS IN WARFARE. The Invasion of Hastings, 1909.
div.p: MOTOR CARS IN WARFARE. The Invasion of Hastings, 1909.

Probably few people locally have realised the importance of the great experiment recently carried out by the War Office in conjunction with the Automobile Association demonstrating the practic- ability of utilizing motors for defensive purpcses. In these days when the possibility of invasion by a foreign foe is so much in cur thoughts—ft stered, we fear, by a section of the press of a sensation-loving type and by certain politicians trying all they know to score off the Government,not for defensive purposes Lut purely from a party political point of view—is is with considerable interest we have watched the recent War Office experiment of proving the use of motor cars for military purposes, by transporting a battalion of Guards ready for action with guns and ammunition in about three hours and without any serious delay from London to Hastings.

Hastings! the last Flue in which a foreign foe landed on our shores. What memories the name revives. William the Conqueror,on whose tomb it has been our privilege to wand in that quaint Normandy city of Caen. 1066, what Briton tut remembers that date; not even the date of the death of our late beloved Queen is more firmly fixed in the memory of the naqon. A Volunteer Motor Transport—the phrase is preg- nant with possibilities for such a country as ours with good roads and many of them, besides the possibility of going almcst as the crow flies carrying your culverts with you, as demonstrated by the great Pekin to Paris race of two years ago. Is the Volunteer destined to remain with us after all, but in another form? The high-minded sportsmanship and patriotism of the average motorist seems to suggest it ! Locally we are specially interested in the recent experiments, as the historic procession some three miles long of nearly 400 motor cars, was headed into Hastings by a Warringtonian, Mr. F. S. Bennett, late of Bewsey Hall. Mr. Bennett had the honour, due we presume, to his magnificent series of successes in all the great reliability trials of recent years, of taking Colonel Gordon Gilmour (commanding officer of the Grenadier Guards), and Captain the Hon. Robert Lygon on his car.

The procession bas not gone many miles through the snowy lanes of Kent, lined by the thousands of interested spectators, when the car in which the General (Sir Francis Stopford) was travelling had an involuntary stop. Mr. Bennett's. car was at once requisitioned and bad the honour of heading the procession with the General and Colonel on board. Except for a quarter-hour stop to give the men a sandwich, and for the General to make an inspection not a moment was subsequently lost and the great procession triumphantly entered Hastings amid the plaudits of the assembled population. To further test the stamina of the men the run back to London was undertaken without a stop of any kind no interval for refreshments being allowed, conse- quently to many the return journey was somewhat chilling especially to such as were unaccustomed to motoring. It is a great tribute to the drivers that no accidents occurred from faulty handling of the cars, although they were running so close together. J.B.

div.head: WARRINGTON CITIZENS' TEMPERANCE LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON CITIZENS' TEMPERANCE LEAGUE.
Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League was held on Wednesday evening in the Winmarleigh Cafe. Owing to the inclement weather there was only a small attendance. Mr. James ' Dodds presided. , Mr. G. A. LEACH, hon. secretary, presented his first annual report and expressed regret that the services had been lost to the executive of Mr. K J. Guest. Mrs. Osborne and Mr. H. Woolley, assistant hon. secretary from ill-health or other causes. Since the formation of the League there had been 32 executive meetings and the average attendance of all members was 14. After reviewing the work accomplished in the way of publio meetings in support of the Government Licensing Bill, Mr. Leach presented the outline of the schera recommended by the executive for widening the scope of the League. They aimed at a membership of at least 1,000 and desired to co-operate with the various local P.S.A.'s, Bible Classes, Bands of Hope, and other kindred organisations in connection with the different churches in the town. It was suggested that those societies might form branches of the league and send their own delegates to the central executive. A good deal of propaganda work was projected and out- door meetings would be held during the summer in the town and suburbs. Special attention would be paid to the forthcoming municipal elections and Mr. Leach hoped that eventually the league would be directly represented on the Town Council. Every member of the General Council was urged to exert himself to increase the membership of the league. In conclusion Mr. Leach tendered with regret his resignation as secretary owing to pressure of other work. The report was discussed and passed and the scheme for the extension of the League's usefulness approved. , A vote of thanks to Mr. Leach for his valuable ,Iservices as Secretary was passed on the motion of the ' Rev. T. MILLER, seconded by the Rev. Ram YosoN,and supported by the Rev. C. HARVEY COOK and Mr. DODDS. Mr. DODDS, the hon. treasurer, presented a financial statement which showed that 45 subscribers had con- tributed £lO2 Bs. 6d. He had paid out .£9B Os. 7d., and with one or two outstanding accounts t‘here was a deficit on the year's work of £lO. Mr. Dodds was unanimously re-elected 'president, the Rev. John Yonge, ,t ice-president ; and the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, chairman of the executive. Mr. F. Gandy was appointed hon. treasurer, and Mr. W. Pilkingtou. hen. secretary in succession to Mr. Leach. Mr. F. Gaudy and Mr. T. Wynskilla, were appointed hon. auditors.

A resolution that represclitatives of every Church and temperance organisation should be invited to send at least three representatives, and that a Central Confer- ence to be held early in September, was passed. The following were elected as the Executive :—The Revs. T. Miller, C. Harvey Cook, J. Buglass, R. E. Letneren, John Yonge ; Messrs. James Dodds, C. E. Parker, E. V. Walker, J. Griffiths, T. Dale, H. Wardmon, E. Osborne, R. Carbett. W. Pilkington, D. Hodge, Arthur Mounfield, J. C. Holland, A. Leach, Mr. and Mrs. Muir, and Mrs. Simpson. A vote of thanks to Mr. Dodds concluded the meeting.

div.head: "JACOBITE LANCASHIRE."
div.p: "JACOBITE LANCASHIRE."

A fascinating period of Lancashire history was dealt with in a highly interesting paper on "Jacobite Lancashire" which Mr. Roland J. A. Sherrey, of Liverpool, read before the Warrington Society at the Old Academy on Monday evening. Mr. Sherrey is a close student of the records of the past and his paper was also notable for its literary ability, the chair- man (Mr. Lofthouse) doing Mr. Sherrey the compli- ment to say that some of the more striking passages reminded him of that model essayist, Lord Macaulay. The loyalty to the Stuart cause of several of the leading Lancashire families was the theme of the paper and although the lecturer had not been able to unearth much concerning Warrington or its immediate neighbourhood, there were one or two local touches which call for special mention. Mr. Shelley made a lengthy reference to an interesting but acrimonious correspondence between the Lord Derby of that day and Lord Delamere, after- wards Earl of Warrington, with regard to raising a militia on behalf of William of Orange. Lord Delamere was an extremely staunch adherent of King William 111., and was absolutely whole-hearted for him,and so did not approve of the cautious methods of Lord Derby, who evidently did not think it wise on the landing of William of Orange to at once declare for him until he saw how the country generally would act. The conduct of Lord Delamere at this period was of such an enthusi- astic and determined character that it has been considered by historians that he was the real means of checkmating any intention of the Paptists and High Tories in Lancashire and Cheshire to appear in arms for King James 11. When the Scots, under the command of General Wills, invaded Lancashire on behalf of the old Pretender in 1715, the Hanoverian forces pushed forward to meet them through Wigan, and the importance of Warrington in their line of communications was emphasised by the fact that the bridge and ford there were very strongly guarded, lest the rebels should succeed in breaking through. The lecturer's opinion was that owing to the ruthless severity with which the rising of 1715 was put down in Lancashire and to the fact that the estates of many of the principal families in the county who had risen on behalf of the Pretender were cDnfiscated, Jacobitism, as anything but a sentiment, might be considered to have received its death blow in this county. This was proved by the fact that when the young Pretender passed through Lancashire some twenty years later, practically not one of the landed gentry joined his standard, so bitter were the recollec- tions of the 1715 rising, "It is a pity" the lecturer concluded "that the royalty evinced throughout long years to the false house of Stuart, was not devoted to a better cause."

An interesting discussion, followed and in reply Mr. Shelley remarked that one of the greatest dangers which menaced England at the present time was the indifference a the masses of the people to great and Tital issues.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS ASSOCIATION.
Medical Inspection of School Children.

Warrington teachers were in conference on Saturday morning when the annual meeting of the local teachers' association was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall. Mr. I. Bowen presided over a large attendance. The CHAIRMAN, in the name of all local teachers, most cordially congratulated Mr. John Upson on his appointment as a Justice of the Peace for the borough. The SECRETARY (Mr. F. H. Longshaw) reported that the membership of the association was 209, an increase of 54 over last year. That gratifying increase, follow- ing that of 38 in 1907, showed the interest and enthusiasm of the teachers in the objects and work of the associa- tion. The committee had taken action with regard to Empire Day celebrations, the superannuation petition to Government, the Children's Cot at the Infirmary, the Warrington Charities Committee, and the Children's Summer Camp. Nearly all the members of the associa- tion volunteered to assist the Education Committee in the feeding of. the poor school children by supervising at the free dinners, and it was satisfactory to know that the committee appreciated their voluntary services. The various school children's sports and games,organized by the teachers, had again been a source of enjoyment „and healthy exercise for the children. A successful year had been end, d by the Treasurer (Mr. John Upson) I becoming president of the Lancashire County Associa- tion and also being appointed a magistrate for the borough. (Applause). The report was adopted. The local SECRETARY of the Benevolent and Orphan Fund (Mr. John Cann) reported that local teachers had raised £lOO during the pest year and which amount worked out to an average of 9s. 7d. per head. Teachers throughout L' b ca shire averaged 7s. id. per head. • Mr. S. \V. JEFVIItY reported that there were now 69 local members of the Teachers' Provident Society compared with five, six years ago. The branch was one of the most valuable assets of the Union, and every teacher should take advantage of the benefits offered by it. The election of officers resulted as follows :—Presi- dent, Mr. J. Armitage; vice-president, Mrs. Stanfield; secretary, Mr. P. H. Longshaw ; treasurer, Mr. J. Upson; press and parliamentary correspondent, Mr. F J. Emson ; secretary B. and 0. Funds, Mr. J. div.head: PRESIDENTS' ADDRESS.
div.p: PRESIDENTS' ADDRESS.

MEDICAL INSPECTION OF scHooL CHILDR EN Mr. J. ARMSTRONG, the new president, congratulated thir association on the fact that this year it attained its majority. He had intended to say a few words on the over-supply of teachers but the matter was so ably dealt with by the President of the Lancashire Associa- tion (Mr. Upson) in his presidential address, that nothing useful to what he had said could be added. It would be s4tisfactory to the members to know that Mr. Runciman's promises to the deputation which he received from the executive of the N.U.T. had been fulfilled. The code for 1909, enforced by a circular to the various local education authorities, mide considerable reductions in the number or children, for which the various grades of teachers were resoonsibie. (Applause.) Toe enforce- ment of the medical inspection of school children marked a new are, They were now slowly bat surely getting down to the treatment of causes instead of effects. The medical inspection of children, even so far as it bad been carried on in 'Warrington, had proved that there were hundreds of children, who were not in normal heiath. That was rather startling, and eas made much more serious by the statement made by the melical expert engaged by the London County Council, that under-feeding or mis- takes in feeding of infante, might be remedied later but that under-feeding or improper feeding during the critical school age, say 8-11 could never be remediad. In cases where neglect was suspected; the child must be watched, the case must be followed up, and the parents warned in no uncertain voice that they must do their duty. But it might be that the parents were too poor to provide the necessary medioil remedies, or surgical appliances, or even the necessary quantity and quality of food, required under the directions of the medical officer. Then in these cases, it was the absolute, and incontrovertible duty of the Local Anthority to pro- vide them with proper safeguards and supervision. On the proposition of Mr. STANSIFIBLD, seconded by Mr. U.esoN, Mr. Armstrong was thanked for his address.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The list."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The list."

A thrilling story of Russian life is the theme of a drama entitled " Tho Nihilist" which has been presented at the Royal Court Theatre this week with considerable success. The authors are Mr. 0. Silverstone, late manager of the Royal Court Theatre, and Mr. Hugh' Montogmery and thAy have succeeded in weaving a play with a rapid succession of exciting incidents and a fund of broad humour. Mr. Silverstone is seen in the leading part of Prince Alexander, a ruthless and unprincipled tyrant, and his portrayal is so highly realistic as to rouse the ire of the " gods." Mr. Silverstone is quite at home on the boards and enters into the action of the drama with plenty of dash and energy. Miss Edna Clare as Alexina Orloff proves a great favourite with the aufience, for she acts with great power and pathos. Mr. William A. Armour achieves a great success as Ivan Novvasky, the noble-hearted village .blacksmith, and Mr. J. Brunelle Harvey presents a clever study of Father Gourko,,the exiled priest. Miss Florrie Kelsey impersonates the imperious Princess Olga in remarkable style. Mr. Connell Clark (Karl Orloff) and Mr. C. Newton Backland (Piertree Petoff) make the most of their parts, and the humorous element, is brightly sustained by Mr. Henry Wright and Miss Jessica Ford.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROC4RANDIE,
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROC4RANDIE,

Next week 11. W. Tebbutt and a M. Copping will present the new romantic drama "Held in Bondage" (by Mr. Robert Castleton). This play also deals with life in Russia and it will be performed by a powerful London company, including Miss Constance Medwyn who has previously figured with much success at tne Court Theatre. There will be elaborate scenery— including a reproduction of the monument of Nicholas II at St. Petersburg—and magnificent dresses and uniforms.
